q: Cookie Monster chokes on a bone in a salmon fillet that a restaurant sold as "boneless." Under which approach is his claim for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability strongest?
o: The foreign-natural test, because a bone is natural to fish.
Under any test, because the restaurant is a merchant.
Neither, because food served in a restaurant is not a sale of goods.
Neither, because the restaurant was not negligent.
None of the above.
oe: Under that test (Webster), a natural bone generally defeats the claim.
Merchant status triggers the warranty but doesn't decide breach. Under the foreign-natural test (Webster), a natural bone defeats the claim.
§ 2-314(1): serving food or drink for value is a sale.
Merchantability is not negligence-based.

Correct. His claim is strongest under the reasonable-expectation test (Mexicali Rose, Schafer), because a diner can reasonably expect a fillet sold as boneless to have no bones. No choice names that test.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Fish bone

q: Which language is sufficient to disclaim the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose if it is in a conspicuous writing?
o: A clear disclaimer of fitness printed in small type on the back of the order form.
"There are no warranties which extend beyond the description on the face hereof."
An oral statement by the salesperson that "this sale has no warranties."
"Seller disclaims the implied warranty of merchantability."
None of the above.
oe: That wouldn't be conspicuous.
Correct. § 2-316(2): a fitness disclaimer must be in writing and conspicuous, but need not mention fitness.
Fitness disclaimers must be written.
That covers merchantability only.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Fitness disclaimer

q: A merchant seller delivers nonconforming goods. The buyer rightfully rejects them after inspection, and they are destroyed while the seller is taking them back to its store. Who bears the risk of loss?
o: It depends on whether the seller had insurance.
The seller, because the tender was nonconforming.
The buyer, until the goods are safely returned to the seller's place of business.
The buyer, because a merchant seller's risk ends once it tenders the goods.
None of the above.
oe: The rule doesn't depend on insurance here.
Correct. § 2-510(1): when a tender so fails to conform as to give a right of rejection, risk stays with the seller until cure or acceptance.
Risk stays with the seller.
That is not the rule for a rightfully rejected tender. § 2-510(1) keeps risk on the seller until cure or acceptance.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Nonconforming goods

q: Buyer accepts goods but fails to pay. What may Seller recover?
o: Damages measured under § 2-708(1), not the price.
The goods themselves, by reclaiming them.
The price, plus incidental damages.
Lost profits under § 2-708(2), but not the price.
None of the above.
oe: Seller may recover the price.
Reclamation is rare (§§ 2-507(2), 2-702(2)).
The price is the remedy.
C is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Action for the price

q: A contract says: "Buyer may not assign its rights under this contract." Buyer assigns its right to receive the goods anyway. What is the likely effect of the clause?
o: The contract is automatically canceled, because Buyer breached.
The assignment is valid, and the clause has no effect at all.
The clause bars only delegation, so Buyer has done nothing wrong.
The assignment is effective, but Buyer may be liable to Seller for breach.
The assignment is void, because the clause expressly forbids it.
oe: Nothing in § 2-210 cancels the contract.
The clause can make the assignment a breach.
That is how § 2-210(4) reads a ban on assigning "the contract," but this clause expressly addresses Buyer's rights.
Correct. Wording like "may not assign" may only make the assignment a breach.
To make an assignment ineffective, the clause should say something like "any attempted assignment is void."
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Ban wording: breach vs. void

q: Which of the following would satisfy the requirement that a merchant's confirmation be "sufficient against the sender" under § 2-201(2)?
o: A signed letter confirming "our widget deal" with no quantity.
A signed price quote for "widgets, quantity to be determined."
An unsigned invoice listing the goods and the price.
"This confirms our deal: 500 widgets at $10. /s/ Seller."
All of the above.
oe: Not sufficient. Quantity is the one essential term.
Not sufficient. A quote does not indicate that a contract was made, and it states no quantity.
Not sufficient. It is not signed by the sender (Problem 2-10(A)).
Correct. It is signed by the sender, indicates a contract was made, and states a quantity, so it satisfies § 2-201(1) against the sender.
Only D is sufficient.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Sufficient against the sender

q: Which of the following statements by a car salesperson is MOST likely to be an express warranty?
o: "This is a great car, and you won't find a better one anywhere."
"This car is the best value you'll find in town this year."
"Parts for this model are readily available locally."
"I think you'll love the way it handles on the highway."
"Trust me, you'll be very happy with this one."
oe: General praise: puffing.
An affirmation of value, which § 2-313(2) excludes.
Correct. It is specific and measurable, so it is likely a warranty (Problem 3-6).
Opinion, hedged with "I think."
Puffing (compare Problem 3-7, "you'll be very happy").
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Specific vs. general

q: Which of the following is NOT a "good" under UCC § 2-105?
o: A certificated share of Microsoft stock.
Calves that have not yet been born.
A gold coin purchased from a coin dealer for a collection.
Kitchen cabinets specially manufactured for the buyer's home.
A crop of soybeans still growing in the field.
oe: Correct. Investment securities are excluded from "goods" (§ 2-105(1)); they are governed by Article 8.
It is a good. § 2-105(1) expressly includes "the unborn young of animals."
It is a good. The coin is the subject of the sale, not "the money in which the price is to be paid" (Problem 1-1).
It is a good. The definition expressly covers "specially manufactured goods."
It is a good. § 2-105(1) includes growing crops, and § 2-107(2) treats them as goods whoever severs them.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — What is a "good"

q: Kermit agrees to sell Fozzie 100 kazoos for $500. Before delivery, Kermit's costs rise, and Fozzie agrees in a signed writing to pay $600 instead. Fozzie later refuses to pay more than $500, arguing he got nothing new in return. What result?
o: Fozzie wins, because Kermit gave no new consideration for the higher price.
Fozzie wins, because the modification needed a new writing signed by both parties.
Kermit wins, provided a court finds the $600 price reasonable.
Kermit wins, because Article 2 modifications need no consideration.
Fozzie wins, because a modification must be made under § 2-207.
oe: § 2-209(1) abolishes the consideration requirement for modifications.
A writing is needed only if the statute of frauds or a NOM clause requires it, and only the party to be charged must sign.
The test is good faith and the formal requirements, not reasonableness of the price.
Correct. § 2-209(1). The modification must still be sought in good faith, and a market shift that makes performance a loss can justify asking (cmt. 2).
§ 2-207 is about the battle of the forms, not modification.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Modification: consideration

q: The buyer claims the seller fraudulently induced the contract by lying about the goods. The writing is complete and exclusive. Can the buyer introduce evidence of the fraud?
o: Yes, unless the writing contains a merger clause.
No, unless the misrepresentation itself was made in writing.
Yes, because the rule does not bar evidence of fraud.
No, because the writing is a complete and exclusive statement of the terms.
None of the above.
oe: A merger clause doesn't bar fraud evidence.
Fraud is usually oral, and the PER doesn't bar evidence of it.
Correct.
The PER does not bar evidence of fraud.
C is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Fraud

q: A contract for 1,000 sacks of feed says the price will be "set by a third party both agree on." The buyer refuses to name anyone. The market price is $13 per sack. What may the seller do?
o: Cancel, or fix a reasonable price itself and sue.
Fix whatever price it chooses, since the buyer is at fault.
Sue for specific performance to make the buyer name someone.
Nothing, because there is no contract without an agreed price.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-305(3): when the price fails to be fixed through one party's fault, the other may cancel or fix a reasonable price. Problem 4-3(c).
It may fix a reasonable price only.
The seller has broader options.
The parties intended to contract.
A is correct.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Price failure through one party's fault

q: Grover orders 100 blue widgets from Elmo "for prompt shipment." Elmo is out of blue widgets, so he promptly ships 100 green widgets without saying anything. What is the legal effect of the shipment?
o: It accepts Grover's offer and is also a breach.
It creates no contract, because the goods do not match the order.
It is an acceptance, and the contract is for green widgets.
It is a counteroffer that Grover may accept or reject.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-206(1)(b): prompt shipment of conforming or nonconforming goods accepts an order for prompt shipment. Without notice of accommodation, the nonconforming shipment is both an acceptance and a breach.
The UCC rejects that mirror-image result for shipments.
The contract is on Grover's terms (blue widgets), so the green widgets are a breach.
That is true only if the seller seasonably notifies the buyer that the shipment is an accommodation.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Formation — Accepting by shipping nonconforming goods

q: Snuffy has bought equipment from Big Bird's Equipment for years, and Big Bird has always delivered it to Snuffy's farm. Their new contract for a skid loader is silent on delivery. Big Bird tells Snuffy to come pick it up. Who is in breach if neither budges?
o: Snuffy, because course of dealing never fills an open term.
Big Bird, because the parties' course of dealing fills the delivery term.
Neither, because the contract is too indefinite to enforce.
Snuffy, because the default place of delivery is the seller's place of business.
None of the above.
oe: Course of dealing explains and supplements the agreement (§ 1-303(d)).
Correct. Problem 3-8(B). No gap means no gap filler.
Open terms don't defeat the contract.
The gap filler applies only if there is a gap; course of dealing fills it first.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Course of dealing fills gap

q: A seller tenders a newer model of a machine than ordered, reasonably believing the buyer will accept it, because it is better and the same price. The buyer rejects. The contract time has expired. Can the seller cure?
o: No, because the contract time for performance has already expired.
Yes, at any time before the buyer covers or sues.
Yes, within a further reasonable time, with seasonable notice.
No, because the buyer's rejection ends the seller's right to cure.
None of the above.
oe: § 2-508(2) gives a further reasonable time.
Only a further reasonable time.
Cure is a response to rejection.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Cure: further reasonable time

q: Big Discount's supplier contract lets Big Discount demand "whatever assurances it deems appropriate, whenever it wishes." Is this clause enforceable?
o: Yes, because the supplier agreed to it in a negotiated contract.
Yes, if the supplier is also a merchant who reviewed the clause.
No, because § 2-609 sets the only standard and the parties cannot change it.
Yes, because parties may vary the Code's provisions by agreement.
No, because it sets an arbitrary rather than a reasonable standard.
oe: Agreement alone isn't enough. Parties may define adequate assurance only by reasonable standards (§ 1-302(b)).
Not the test.
They may, if reasonably.
Arbitrary standards are not enforceable.
Correct. § 2-609 cmt. 6; § 1-302(b); Problem 6-4.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Arbitrary standard

q: Between merchants, how are reasonable grounds for insecurity and the adequacy of an assurance judged?
o: According to commercial standards.
By whether the assurance is in a notarized writing.
By the subjective feelings of the insecure party.
By whether the assurance includes a letter of credit.
By the court's own sense of fairness.
oe: No formality is required.
The test is objective.
A letter of credit is one common assurance, not the test.
The Code uses commercial standards.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Commercial standards

q: Under Official Comment 3 to § 2-313, what must a buyer show about reliance to recover for breach of an express warranty?
o: That the buyer's reliance on the statement was reasonable.
That the buyer relied solely on the seller's statement.
Nothing in particular; such affirmations are presumed part of the bargain.
That the buyer read the warranty before signing the contract.
None of the above.
oe: Not required by Comment 3.
Comment 3 says no particular reliance need be shown.
Correct. Courts split (reliance, no reliance, rebuttable presumption), but Comment 3 is the Code's own position.
Warranties in written contracts, and even owner's manuals read after the sale, can count.
C is correct.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Basis of the bargain

q: Gonzo agrees to sell Rowlf the right to drill for and remove the natural gas under Gonzo's farm. Rowlf will do all the drilling and extraction. Is this a sale of goods governed by Article 2?
o: Yes, because the parties may agree that Article 2 governs.
Yes, because natural gas becomes movable once it is extracted.
Yes, because things attached to realty are goods if they can be removed.
No, because the seller will not be severing the gas.
No, because extraction rights are a service, not a sale.
oe: The parties' choice of law is the last of the four factors. It cannot turn an interest in land into a sale of goods.
Gas is movable once extracted, but § 2-107(1) adds a condition for minerals: the seller must sever them.
Too broad. § 2-107 treats only certain things attached to realty as goods, and minerals only when the seller severs them.
Correct. Under § 2-107(1), oil, gas, and other minerals are goods only if the seller severs them. Here the buyer extracts, so it is an interest in land (Problem 1-1).
It isn't a service contract. The problem is who severs the gas.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Minerals: who severs

q: A seller gives an express warranty about a machine's speed. The buyer also had a particular purpose that the seller knew about and relied on. If the express warranty and the implied warranties are inconsistent, which statement is correct under § 2-317?
o: Implied warranties control, since they arise by operation of law.
A sample controls over exact specifications if the two conflict.
Express warranties displace inconsistent implied warranties, except fitness.
Express warranties displace all inconsistent implied warranties, fitness included.
None of the above.
oe: The reverse, except for fitness.
Exact specifications displace an inconsistent sample (§ 2-317(a)).
Correct. § 2-317(c).
Fitness for a particular purpose is the exception.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Cumulation

q: Which of the following is NOT an element of the specially manufactured goods exception to the statute of frauds?
o: The seller has made a substantial beginning of manufacture or commitments for procurement.
The seller's beginning occurred before notice of repudiation was received.
The buyer has paid for at least part of the goods before the seller began work.
The goods are not suitable for sale to others in the ordinary course of the seller's business.
The goods are to be specially manufactured for the buyer.
oe: Required.
Required.
Correct. Payment is not an element of § 2-201(3)(a). Payment and acceptance matter to the part-performance exception (§ 2-201(3)(c)).
Required.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Specially manufactured goods

q: In Roth Steel v. Sharon Steel, why was the price modification unenforceable?
o: Because it lacked consideration from Roth for the higher price.
Because Roth was not a merchant, so a stricter good-faith rule applied.
Because a market shift is not a legitimate reason to seek a modification.
Because it was not in a writing signed by Roth.
Because Sharon extracted it by threatening to stop selling to Roth.
oe: Consideration isn't needed (§ 2-209(1)).
Both were merchants.
The court found Sharon passed the objective test: the market shift gave it a legitimate commercial reason.
The case turned on good faith, not on a writing.
Correct. Good faith has two parts: an objective reason and honesty in fact. Extracting the change by threatening to breach failed the subjective prong.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Roth Steel

q: In Webster v. Blue Ship Tea Room (cited in the casebook), a diner was injured by a fish bone in fish chowder. What was the outcome?
o: The restaurant won, because bones are natural to fish chowder.
The diner won, because a bone in chowder breaches merchantability.
The restaurant won, because restaurants make no warranties.
The diner won, because the restaurant should have strained the chowder.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Webster is the classic "foreign-natural" case.
The court reversed the jury verdict for the diner.
Food served for value is a sale (§ 2-314(1)); the restaurant won on the merits.
The claim was for breach of warranty, not negligence, and the diner lost.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Webster

q: Gonzo accepts a motorcycle, then rightfully revokes his acceptance because of a serious defect. Before the seller picks it up, it is stolen from Gonzo's garage. Gonzo's insurance covers $3,000 of the $10,000 loss. Who bears the remaining $7,000?
o: Gonzo, because the motorcycle was in his possession.
The seller, but only to the extent Gonzo's insurance falls short.
The seller, for the full $10,000, regardless of insurance.
Gonzo, because he accepted the motorcycle before revoking.
None of the above.
oe: § 2-510(2) treats the risk as on the seller to the extent of the buyer's insurance gap.
Only to the extent of the insurance deficiency.
Rightful revocation shifts the risk back.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Revocation and insurance

q: A letter of intent for the sale of a machine says: "The parties do not intend to be bound unless and until they agree on a price." They never agree, but the seller has already delivered the machine and the buyer has paid a deposit. What is the result?
o: No contract; each side must return what it received.
The buyer keeps the machine and gets its deposit back.
A contract at the seller's list price, since it delivered first.
A contract at a reasonable price at the time of delivery.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-305(4): the buyer returns the machine (or pays its reasonable value if it can't), and the seller returns the deposit.
Each side returns what it received.
There is no contract.
That applies only if the parties intended to contract without a settled price.
A is correct.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Intent not to be bound

q: Buyer rightfully rejects a shipment of tables that are in its possession. Which statement about Buyer's duties is correct?
o: Buyer may use the tables until Seller gets around to picking them up.
Buyer must hold them with reasonable care for Seller to remove.
Buyer must ship the tables back to Seller, at Seller's expense.
Buyer may sell the tables and keep the proceeds for itself.
None of the above.
oe: Using them would be exercising ownership, which is wrongful.
The buyer has no duty to ship them back. It need only hold them with reasonable care (or follow reasonable instructions).
Merchant buyers may resell perishables or follow instructions (§§ 2-603, 2-604), but not keep proceeds as their own.
B is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Duties after rejection

q: Rosita orders 100 blue widgets from Herry "for prompt shipment." Herry is out of blue widgets, so he promptly ships 100 green widgets and the same day emails Rosita: "We're out of blue. Sending green as an accommodation." What is the effect of the shipment?
o: The shipment is an acceptance, but Herry may cure by shipping blue widgets later.
The shipment is an acceptance and a breach.
The shipment is an acceptance, and the notice modifies the contract to green widgets.
Rosita must keep the green widgets and pay for them.
None of the above.
oe: The shipment is not an acceptance at all, because Herry seasonably notified Rosita that it was only an accommodation.
That is the result without the notice.
No contract was formed, so there is nothing to modify.
Rosita may reject the counteroffer.

Correct. Because Herry seasonably notified Rosita that the green widgets were offered only as an accommodation, the shipment is not an acceptance (§ 2-206(1)(b)). It is a counteroffer that Rosita may accept or reject.
topic: 2 · Formation — Accommodation shipment

q: Under § 2-106, what is the difference between "termination" and "cancellation"?
o: Cancellation discharges executory duties; termination does not.
Cancellation is for the other side's breach; termination is for some other reason.
Nothing; the Code uses the two terms interchangeably.
Termination is for the other side's breach; cancellation is for some other reason.
Termination preserves remedies for breach; cancellation does not.
oe: Both discharge executory duties.
The Code defines them differently.
Reversed.
A cancelling party keeps its remedies for breach of the whole contract or unperformed balance.
topic: 14 · Termination — Termination vs. cancellation

q: Fozzie buys a used car "AS IS," stated conspicuously in the written contract. The transmission fails. Which implied warranties have been disclaimed?
o: None, because "as is" must mention merchantability.
Both merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose.
Only merchantability, because "as is" says nothing about fitness.
Merchantability, fitness, and the warranty of title.
Only fitness, because merchantability must be mentioned by name.
oe: The "as is" exception doesn't require that.
"As is" disclaims all implied warranties.
Title isn't disclaimed by "as is."
All implied warranties.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — As is

q: Which merger clause best tracks § 2-202(b) to make a writing a complete integration?
o: "This writing represents the final agreement of the parties."
"This agreement supersedes all prior agreements between the parties, written or oral."
"This agreement may not be modified except by a signed writing."
"This writing is the complete and exclusive statement of our agreement."
None of the above.
oe: Only a partial integration.
Helpful, but misses contemporaneous terms.
That's a NOM clause.
Correct. Problem 5-11, clause 2.
D is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Merger clause wording

q: Buyer rightfully rejects defective machines and pays $800 to store them while awaiting the seller's instructions. Buyer also loses $20,000 in profits because its production line is shut down, which seller had reason to know at contracting. How are these damages classified?
o: Both are incidental, because both resulted from the breach.
Both are consequential, because seller had reason to know of them.
The storage cost is consequential, and the lost profits are incidental.
The storage cost is incidental, and the lost profits are consequential.
None of the above.
oe: Lost profits are consequential.
Storage is incidental.
Reversed. Costs of responding to the breach are incidental; losses from the buyer's needs are consequential.
Correct. § 2-715(1) (incidental: costs of responding to breach) and § 2-715(2) (consequential: losses from needs seller had reason to know).
D is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Incidental vs. consequential

q: Gobo's Gadgets has supplied Red's Hardware for years under an arrangement with no stated duration and no termination clause. Gobo wants to stop. May Gobo end the arrangement?
o: Yes, at any time and without notice, since no duration was set.
Yes, but only with reasonable notification to Red's.
No, because an arrangement with no end date continues until breach.
Yes, after giving a full year's notice, the default for open-ended supply deals.
Only if Gobo has a legitimate business reason for ending it.
oe: Reasonable notification is required.
Correct. § 2-309(2)–(3). Reasonable notice means enough time for Red's to find a substitute supplier.
§ 2-309(2): an indefinite contract is valid for a reasonable time but may be terminated at any time.
The standard is reasonable notice, not a fixed period.
No reason is needed (Santa Fe).
topic: 14 · Termination — Indefinite duration

q: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for a buyer to recover consequential damages for lost profits under § 2-715(2)?
o: The loss could not reasonably have been prevented by cover or otherwise.
The loss resulted from the seller's breach.
The seller expressly agreed to be liable for consequential damages.
The seller had reason to know of the buyer's needs at the time of contracting.
None of the above.
oe: Required.
Required.
Correct. No express agreement is needed; reason to know is enough.
Required.
C is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Consequential: limits

q: Grover's buyer has always paid on time, and nothing suggests any problem. Grover nonetheless writes: "Pay the full price in advance or we won't ship." Under the § 2-609 flowchart, what is the risk to Grover?
o: None, because a party may demand assurance whenever it chooses.
Without reasonable grounds, his demand may itself be a repudiation.
None, so long as the demand is made in writing.
The buyer must prepay within 30 days or it will be in breach.
None, because a mere demand for assurance cannot be a repudiation.
oe: Reasonable grounds for insecurity are required.
Correct. The § 2-609/§ 2-610 flowchart.
A writing is necessary, not sufficient; grounds are also required.
The buyer's duty arises only after a justified demand.
It is a repudiation when performance is conditioned on it.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Demand without grounds

q: Before the sale, the seller demands that the buyer inspect a used tractor, but the buyer refuses. The tractor has a cracked engine block that an inspection would have revealed. Does the buyer have a merchantability claim for the crack?
o: Yes, because a buyer's inspection is optional before the sale.
No, because he refused the seller's demand that he inspect.
Yes, because the seller is a merchant with respect to tractors.
No, because a used tractor carries no implied warranties.
None of the above.
oe: The buyer's choice has consequences.
The buyer's refusal matters.
Used goods can carry warranties.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Refusal to examine

q: A contract prices wheat at "the Chicago Board price on March 15." The board is closed on March 15. The last price, on March 13, was $12. What is the price?
o: A reasonable price at delivery, likely about $12.
The seller may cancel, because the agreed price was never fixed.
There is no contract, because the agreed standard failed.
Whatever price the buyer reasonably chooses.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-3(b).
Cancellation is for a price that fails through one party's fault (§ 2-305(3)). The board closing was no one's fault.
If the parties intended to contract, a reasonable price applies (§ 2-305(1)(c)).
No party gets to choose.
A is correct.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Agreed standard fails

q: What is the effect of a merger clause?
o: It conclusively establishes complete integration.
It turns a partial integration into a complete integration as a matter of law.
It bars evidence of fraud.
It bars later modifications.
None of the above.
oe: It is probative, not conclusive.
A merger clause is evidence of complete integration, not conclusive proof.
The PER never bars fraud evidence.
That's a NOM clause.

Correct. A merger clause is probative, not conclusive, evidence that the writing is a complete integration. It never bars evidence of fraud, and it says nothing about later modifications (that is a NOM clause).
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Merger clause effect

q: Unless the offer unambiguously indicates otherwise, how may an offer to make a contract for the sale of goods be accepted under § 2-206(1)(a)?
o: Only in the same medium the offeror used to make the offer.
Only by beginning performance within a reasonable time.
Only by a signed writing that states the quantity.
In any manner and by any medium reasonable in the circumstances.
Only by a prompt promise to ship or a prompt shipment.
oe: That is not the UCC rule. Acceptance may be in any reasonable manner and medium.
Beginning performance is one possible mode, not the only one.
No writing is needed to accept, though the statute of frauds may require a record for enforcement.
Correct. § 2-206(1)(a). The offeror can still be "master of the offer" by unambiguously requiring a particular manner.
That is § 2-206(1)(b), which covers orders for prompt or current shipment. Under (1)(a), any reasonable manner and medium will do.
topic: 2 · Formation — Medium of acceptance

q: A seller has identified conforming goods to the contract. The buyer repudiates. A week later, while the seller is still looking for another buyer, the goods are destroyed. The seller's insurance covers half the loss. Who bears the other half?
o: The buyer, but only to the extent of the seller's insurance deficiency.
The seller, because the repudiation ended the contract.
The buyer, for the full loss, because it repudiated.
The seller, because it still had the goods in its possession.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-510(3): risk rests on the repudiating buyer for a commercially reasonable time, to the extent of any deficiency in the seller's insurance.
Repudiation doesn't end the buyer's exposure.
Only to the extent of the insurance deficiency.
§ 2-510(3) shifts risk to the breaching buyer.
A is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Buyer repudiates

q: Mokey buys 20 skeins of yarn and finds the color varies slightly among the five dye lots. The variation is within what the yarn trade permits. Has the seller breached the warranty of merchantability?
o: Yes, because merchantable goods must be of identical color and quality.
Yes, because a merchant seller warrants uniformity among lots.
No, because the variation is within what trade usage permits.
No, because color is a matter of taste rather than quality.
None of the above.
oe: § 2-314(2)(d) allows variations permitted by the agreement.
Being a merchant triggers the warranty but doesn't mean it was breached.
Correct. Problem 3-10.
That isn't the reason. The test is whether the variation is within what the agreement, including trade usage, permits.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Yarn dye lots

q: Count, a consumer, signs a merchant's preprinted sales form that includes a clause requiring all modifications to be in a signed writing. Count does not separately sign the clause. Later, the merchant and Count orally agree to change the delivery date. Is the NOM clause enforceable against Count?
o: Yes, because Count signed the form that contains it.
Yes, because the delivery date is a material term.
No, because the UCC does not enforce NOM clauses.
No, because Count did not separately sign it.
None of the above.
oe: On a form supplied by a merchant, the non-merchant must separately sign the NOM clause (§ 2-209(2)).
Materiality has nothing to do with whether the NOM clause binds Count.
The UCC reverses the common law; NOM clauses are enforceable.
D is correct.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — NOM clause and non-merchant

q: A buyer rejects a shipment, saying only "These are unacceptable." The defect was a wrong label the seller could have easily fixed. Later, the buyer tries to rely on the labeling defect to justify the rejection. What result?
o: No, because it failed to state a defect the seller could have cured.
Yes, because a buyer may rely on any defect it discovers later, stated or not.
Yes, but the seller must first be given a chance to cure.
No, because the rejection was oral rather than written.
None of the above.
oe: Unstated curable defects are lost.
The buyer's failure to particularize is the issue.
Rejection need not be in writing. The problem is that the buyer didn't state the curable defect.
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Failure to particularize

q: In a deposition, Oscar admits that he orally agreed to buy 200 trash cans from Telly, although Telly claims the deal was for 300. There is no signed record. To what extent is the contract enforceable against Oscar?
o: Not at all, because there is no signed record.
Up to 250 trash cans, splitting the difference between the two claims.
Up to 300 trash cans, because Oscar admitted a contract exists.
Up to 300 trash cans, if Telly proves that quantity at trial.
None of the above.
oe: The admission exception applies (§ 2-201(3)(b)).
There is no compromise rule.
Enforcement is limited to the quantity admitted.
Even then, the exception stops at the admitted quantity.
Correct. The contract is enforceable against Oscar up to 200 trash cans, the quantity he admitted in court (§ 2-201(3)(b)). No choice states that.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Admission

q: Siebenmann sells Rogath a painting with a written warranty that it is authentic. Before the sale, Rogath hears from a museum curator (not from Siebenmann) that the painting's authenticity is doubted. The painting is a fake. Under Rogath v. Siebenmann, can Rogath recover for breach of warranty?
o: Yes, but Rogath must show he relied on the warranty when buying.
No, because Rogath did not believe the warranty when he bought.
Yes, because he may have bought the warranty as insurance.
No, because Rogath waived the warranty by closing despite the doubts.
None of the above.
oe: Rogath treats the warranty as risk allocation, not as a reliance test.
The question is whether the buyer bought the seller's promise, not whether he believed it.
Correct. Rogath held that a buyer who learns doubts from a third party or from common knowledge can still enforce the warranty.
Waiver arises only when the seller himself disclosed the facts that made the warranty false.
C is correct.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Rogath: third-party knowledge

q: Waldorf contracts to sell Statler all of the standing timber on Waldorf's land. The contract says Statler will cut and haul the trees himself. Does Article 2 apply?
o: Yes, because Statler is a merchant in timber.
No, because the buyer, not the seller, will sever the timber.
No, because standing timber is part of the real estate.
Yes, but only after the timber is cut.
None of the above.
oe: Merchant status never decides whether Article 2 applies (Problem 1-4).
That is the rule for minerals and structures (§ 2-107(1)), not timber.
§ 2-107(2) treats timber to be cut as goods even while it stands.
The contract is for the sale of goods from the start. § 2-107(2) applies to the contract to sell timber to be cut.

Correct. Article 2 applies, but for a reason none of the choices gives: timber to be cut is a good whether the buyer or the seller severs it (§ 2-107(2)). B states the rule for minerals and structures, not timber.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Timber: either party severs

q: Herry buys a camera from a camera store, explaining that he needs a battery that lasts four hours for wedding shoots. The clerk recommends this model. The battery lasts one hour, which is normal for this camera. Which warranty is most clearly breached?
o: The warranty of good title and against encumbrances.
The warranty against infringement of third-party patents.
The implied warranty of merchantability under § 2-314.
The implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose (§ 2-315).
None of the above.
oe: Title would be breached if the camera were stolen. Nothing suggests that.
No infringement claim here.
A one-hour battery may be normal for this camera, so it may be fit for ordinary purposes.
Correct. This is the outline's camera example: a battery that won't last the four hours the buyer needs breaches § 2-315.
D is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Which warranty

q: Unless the parties otherwise agree, when is the buyer obligated to pay for the goods?
o: When the contract is signed, unless credit is extended.
When the seller ships the goods to the buyer.
When and where the buyer receives the goods.
Whenever the seller demands payment after contracting.
Within 30 days after the goods are delivered.
oe: No credit or prepayment is presumed either way; payment is due on receipt.
Payment is due on receipt, not shipment (§ 2-310(a)).
Correct. § 2-310(a).
The seller can't set the time unilaterally.
There is no 30-day default rule; no credit is presumed.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Payment timing

q: A seller gives a written warranty that a painting is authentic. Before closing, the seller himself tells the buyer that experts have doubted the painting's authenticity. The buyer closes anyway without saying anything to preserve its rights. Under Rogath v. Siebenmann, what is the most likely result?
o: The buyer recovers, because no reliance on the warranty need be shown.
The buyer waived the breach by closing without preserving its rights.
The buyer recovers, because the warranty was in a signed writing.
The buyer recovers half its loss, since both parties knew of the doubts.
None of the above.
oe: Reliance isn't the issue; waiver is.
Correct. That is why the source of the buyer's knowledge decided Rogath, and why the case was remanded for trial on who told Rogath.
A writing doesn't stop waiver.
There is no splitting rule.
B is correct.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Rogath: seller's own disclosure

q: Rowlf sells custom goods to a buyer whose credit has been downgraded and who has been paying other suppliers late. Rowlf sends a proper § 2-609 demand. The buyer replies only: "Don't worry, we'll pay." Which statement is most accurate?
o: The bare promise is adequate, since the buyer has never missed a payment to Rowlf.
Rowlf may insist on a letter of credit and refuse any other assurance.
Rowlf must ship now, because the buyer responded within 30 days.
A bare promise is likely inadequate, but real proof of solvency could suffice.
None of the above.
oe: Given these grounds, a bare promise from a shaky buyer is likely inadequate.
A letter of credit is common (Top of Iowa), but insisting only on it may be too much.
A timely reply isn't enough. It must also be adequate.
Correct. Problem 6-3(b). Adequacy depends on the party's reputation and the facts (§ 2-609 cmt. 4).
D is correct.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Adequacy of a bare promise

q: Seller sends Buyer a proposal (the offer). Buyer responds with a purchase order whose boilerplate says acceptance is "expressly limited to such terms" as appear in the purchase order. The forms differ on several terms. Under Daitom v. Pennwalt, is Buyer's purchase order an acceptance?
o: Yes, because that boilerplate does not make acceptance expressly conditional.
No, because it varies the offer's terms, so it is a counteroffer.
No, because it is expressly conditional on Seller's assent to Buyer's terms.
Yes, and Buyer's terms control because Buyer sent the last form.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Daitom (following Dorton) treated the purchase order as a definite and seasonable expression of acceptance under § 2-207(1).
§ 2-207(1) abolishes the mirror-image rule for sales of goods.
Daitom held that language like "expressly limited to such terms" is not enough. The offeree must clearly show it is unwilling to proceed unless its terms are accepted.
§ 2-207 also abolishes the "last shot" rule.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Formation — Daitom: expressly conditional

q: Telly sells his old bicycle to his neighbor Zoe at a yard sale for $40. Neither of them has ever sold a bicycle before. Does Article 2 govern the sale?
o: No, because the bicycle is used rather than new goods.
No, because the price is under the $500 threshold.
Yes, but the sale must be evidenced by a writing.
No, because Article 2 requires at least one merchant.
Yes, because Article 2 applies to transactions in goods.
oe: Used goods are still goods.
The $500 figure is the statute of frauds threshold (§ 2-201), not a limit on Article 2's scope.
Writing goes to enforceability under § 2-201 (and this sale is under $500 anyway), not to scope.
Article 2's scope never depends on merchant status (Problem 1-4). Merchant status matters for particular rules, such as § 2-314.
Correct. Article 2 covers merchant-to-merchant, merchant-to-consumer, consumer-to-merchant, and consumer-to-consumer sales (Problem 1-4).
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Garage sale: scope ignores merchant status

q: A state has adopted Alternative A of § 2-318. Herry buys a toaster from a store. It shorts out and burns Herry's houseguest, who was making breakfast. Can the guest sue the store for breach of warranty?
o: No, because the guest is not in privity of contract with the store.
Yes, because Alternative A covers anyone reasonably expected to be affected.
No, because Alternative A is limited to the buyer's family members.
Yes, because a guest in the buyer's home injured in person is covered.
None of the above.
oe: § 2-318 extends warranties beyond the buyer.
That describes Alternative C (or B, for natural persons injured in person).
Alternative A also covers household members and guests in the home.
Correct. A houseguest injured in person is covered.
D is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Privity: Alternative A

q: A shutter maker makes huge investments to supply Home Depot under an indefinite, at-will arrangement. Home Depot terminates with reasonable notice before the investments pay off. Under Santa Fe Custom Shutters v. Home Depot, can the shutter maker recover five years of lost profits for the termination?
o: Yes, because the arrangement had not run for a reasonable time.
Yes, because the shutter maker relied on the relationship.
No, because the duty of good faith doesn't apply to terminations.
Yes, because good faith requires a good reason to terminate.
No, because no good reason is needed to end an indefinite contract.
oe: The court rejected the argument that the contract must first run a reasonable time.
Reliance doesn't change the at-will nature of the arrangement.
Good faith does apply to termination; it just doesn't override the right to terminate.
Good faith can't contradict an express or statutory right.
Correct. The trial court's five-year lost-profits award was error. Claims for fraud in the inducement, breaches before termination, and unreasonable notice remained.
topic: 14 · Termination — Santa Fe

q: A person who is not a merchant sells goods he knows have a hidden defect. Which statement best describes his obligations?
o: He makes the implied warranty of merchantability, like any seller.
No merchantability warranty, but a duty to disclose the known defect.
He has no obligations, because he is not a merchant.
He is strictly liable for the defect, whether or not he knew of it.
None of the above.
oe: Only merchants do.
Correct. Isolated sellers aren't merchants, but must disclose known material hidden defects.
Comment 3 imposes a duty to disclose known hidden defects.
Strict liability under § 2-314 applies to merchants.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Merchant's duty to disclose

q: Which of the following is a consequence of a buyer's acceptance of goods?
o: The buyer automatically waives damages for nonconformity.
The buyer may still reject the goods for any nonconformity.
The buyer must notify the seller of any breach within a reasonable time.
The seller bears the burden of proving the goods conformed.
None of the above.
oe: Acceptance doesn't impair other remedies (§ 2-607(2)).
Acceptance ends the right to reject (§ 2-607(2)).
The burden shifts to the buyer (§ 2-607(4)).
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — After acceptance

q: Elmo and Zoe orally agree that Elmo will sell Zoe a desk for $400. Before delivery they orally agree to add a matching chair and raise the price to $800. Is the modification enforceable?
o: No, because the original contract was oral, so it can't be modified orally.
Yes, because the original contract did not need a record.
Yes, because a modification needs no new consideration.
No, because the modified deal needs a record and has none.
None of the above.
oe: The original $400 contract needed no record.
What matters is the contract as modified (§ 2-209(3)).
True, but § 2-209(3) also requires the contract as modified to satisfy the statute of frauds.
Correct. Problem 3-4(a). The failed modification may still operate as a waiver.
D is correct.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Modification and SOF: up to $800

q: What is the difference between the parol evidence rule and the statute of frauds?
o: The PER applies only to consumer contracts.
The PER requires a writing; the SOF bars evidence of terms.
Nothing; they are two names for the same rule.
The PER governs what evidence of terms comes in; the SOF, enforceability.
None of the above.
oe: It applies to any writing the parties intended as final.
Reversed and garbled. The SOF requires a record for enforcement; the PER bars evidence of certain terms.
They answer different questions: what evidence comes in, and whether the contract can be enforced at all.
Correct.
D is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — PER vs. SOF

q: A seller's contract states that the goods are "100% wool" and also states "Seller makes no warranties, express or implied." The goods are 50% wool. Which statement is correct?
o: The disclaimer is effective, so the seller made no warranty at all.
The disclaimer is inoperative to the extent it conflicts with the warranty.
The disclaimer is effective because it appears in the signed written contract.
The express warranty is void, because the disclaimer negates it.
None of the above.
oe: A disclaimer that can't be reconciled with an express warranty is inoperative.
A writing doesn't help.
The disclaimer, not the warranty, gives way.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Express warranty disclaimer

q: Bert orally agrees to buy 10 pigeon coops from Ernie at $100 each. Bert pays for 4 coops, and Ernie delivers them, and Bert accepts them. Ernie then refuses to deliver the rest. Bert sues for the other 6. What result?
o: Bert loses entirely, and he must return the 4 coops he accepted.
Bert wins, because part performance takes the whole contract outside the statute.
Bert loses as to the 6 coops not yet paid for and accepted.
Bert wins, because each coop costs well under $500.
None of the above.
oe: The contract is enforceable as to the 4 coops paid for and accepted.
Part performance validates the contract only for the goods paid for and accepted (or received and accepted).
Correct. § 2-201(3)(c). The deal for 10 coops at $1,000 is within the statute of frauds, and there is no record for the other 6.
The $500 threshold looks at the price of the contract ($1,000), not the price per unit.
C is correct.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Part performance

q: A contract for a commercial oven says the seller will pay $1,000 per day of late delivery. The parties, both merchants, negotiated the clause based on profit discussions. Delivery is 30 days late; actual lost profit is $2,500. Is the clause enforceable?
o: Yes, if reasonable in light of the anticipated harm.
Likely yes, because LD clauses are always enforceable between merchants.
No, because an LD clause must be conspicuous to be enforced.
No, because the amount is twelve times the actual loss.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Problem 5-6. An LD clause is valid if reasonable in light of the anticipated or actual harm, and merchants negotiated this one to cover hard-to-prove harm. The seller will argue the gap makes it a penalty.
They must still be reasonable.
They need not be.
The test looks at anticipated or actual harm.
A is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Liquidated damages

q: Goods are stored in a warehouse, and the seller does not intend to move them. When does the risk of loss pass to the buyer if the warehouse has issued a negotiable warehouse receipt?
o: When the buyer receives the negotiable warehouse receipt.
When the buyer physically takes the goods from the warehouse.
A reasonable time after the seller tells the buyer where the goods are.
When the contract for sale is signed by both parties.
None of the above.
oe: Physical possession isn't required.
That's closer to the rule for non-negotiable documents.
Not under § 2-509(2).
A is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Bailee: negotiable document

q: Elmo and Zoe orally agree to a sale of 100 units for $1,000. Before delivery they orally agree to reduce the order to 40 units for $400. Is the modification enforceable?
o: Yes, because the contract as modified is under $500.
No, because the modification lacks new consideration.
No, because a reduction in quantity must be in a signed writing.
No, because the original contract was for $500 or more.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Problem 3-4(b). § 2-209(3) asks whether the contract as modified is within § 2-201.
No consideration is needed (§ 2-209(1)).
Only if the modified contract is within the statute of frauds.
What matters is the contract as modified.
A is correct.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Modification and SOF: down to $400

q: Under § 2-718(1), an unreasonably large liquidated damages term is:
o: enforceable if both parties are merchants.
reduced to a reasonable amount by the court.
enforceable if the buyer is a consumer.
enforceable if conspicuous.
void as a penalty.
oe: Not if unreasonable.
The term is void.
The buyer's status doesn't save an unreasonably large LD term.
Conspicuousness doesn't matter.
Correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Penalty

q: Goods held by a warehouse without any document of title are sold. When does the risk of loss pass?
o: When the seller pays the warehouse's storage fees.
When the warehouse acknowledges the buyer's right to the goods.
When the buyer pays the full price for the goods.
When the seller tells the buyer the warehouse's address and lot number.
When the contract of sale is made.
oe: Who pays storage has nothing to do with when risk passes under § 2-509(2).
Payment doesn't pass risk.
Telling the buyer where the goods are isn't enough; the warehouse must acknowledge the buyer's right to possession.
Not under § 2-509(2).
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Bailee: acknowledgment

q: Which body of law governs a lease of goods?
o: UCC Article 2.
The common law.
The CISG.
UCC Article 9.
UCC Article 2A.
oe: Article 2 governs sales of goods.
The common law governs gifts of goods.
The CISG governs certain international sales, not leases.
Article 9 governs security interests, including a "lease" that is really a disguised security interest, but not a true lease.
Correct. The slide chart: sale → Article 2 (or CISG); lease → Article 2A; security interest → Article 9; gift → common law.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Which law: lease, gift, security interest

q: In Daitom v. Pennwalt, the seller's offer required any suit within one year of delivery. The buyer's acceptance reserved "all of its rights and remedies available at law." How did the court resolve the conflict?
o: No contract was formed, because the forms conflicted on a material term.
Both terms dropped out, and the Code's four-year limit applied.
A one-year limitations period applied as a reasonable compromise.
The seller's one-year term controlled because the seller's form was the offer.
The buyer's term controlled because the buyer sent the last form.
oe: The purchase order was an acceptance under § 2-207(1), so a contract was formed.
Correct. Applying the knockout rule (§ 2-207 cmt. 6), the court let both terms drop out and filled the gap with § 2-725.
Courts do not split the difference. The gap filler applies.
The court did not let the offeror's term win automatically.
§ 2-207 abolished the last-shot rule.
topic: 2 · Formation — Daitom: knockout

q: In Casazza v. Kiser, the buyer argued that the seller's acceptance of payment for a navigation software license satisfied the part-performance exception for the sale of a sailboat. Why did the court reject that argument?
o: Because the software and the boat were not a single commercial unit.
Because Article 2 does not apply to sales between individuals.
Because promissory estoppel is the only exception to the statute of frauds.
Because the seller had admitted the contract in his deposition.
Because the software license was never signed by the seller.
oe: Correct. The software was bought years after the boat and the boat was later sold without it, so part performance as to the software didn't reach the boat.
Article 2 applied even though both parties were individuals.
The court rejected promissory estoppel too.
The buyer only hoped the seller would admit the deal; there was no admission.
The license was the one document both parties did sign.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Casazza

q: Which version of § 2-318 extends a seller's warranty to a business that suffers only property damage, not personal injury?
o: Alternative C.
Alternative B.
Alternative A.
All of them.
None of them.
oe: Correct. C covers any person reasonably expected to be affected and injured by the breach, not limited to personal injury.
B covers natural persons injured in person.
A covers family, household, and home guests injured in person.
Only Alternative C reaches property damage to a business.
Alternative C does.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Privity: Alternative C

q: Rowlf accepts a piano and uses it for a month. He then discovers a crack in the soundboard that could not have been found on ordinary inspection and that substantially impairs the piano's value. What can Rowlf do?
o: Reject the piano, because it fails to conform in any respect.
Revoke his acceptance, but he needs the seller's agreement.
Nothing, because he accepted the piano and used it.
Revoke his acceptance for the hidden, substantial defect.
None of the above.
oe: Rejection is unavailable after acceptance.
The seller's agreement isn't needed.
Revocation is available for latent defects.
Correct. § 2-608.
D is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Revocation

q: A used-car buyer was told orally: "This car has never been in an accident." The signed contract says "AS IS — NO WARRANTY, EXPRESS OR IMPLIED," and the writing appears final on warranties. The car had been in an accident. What is the buyer's best route?
o: Breach of express warranty, because § 2-316(1) makes the disclaimer inoperative.
Breach of the implied warranty of merchantability.
Fraud, because the parol evidence rule doesn't bar evidence of fraud.
Nothing, because the "as is" clause bars every claim.
None of the above.
oe: § 2-316(1) is subject to § 2-202; if the writing is final on warranties, the oral warranty is excluded.
"As is" kills the implied warranties.
Correct. Problem 5-13.
Fraud is still available.
C is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Used car: oral warranty vs. as is

q: Which statement about whether a disclaimer is "conspicuous" is correct?
o: Fine print is conspicuous if the buyer signs directly below it.
The jury decides, based on how a reasonable buyer would read it.
It is conspicuous if a reasonable person ought to have noticed it.
It is conspicuous whenever it appears in the signed contract.
None of the above.
oe: Not by itself.
It is a question for the court.
Correct. § 1-201(b)(10): for example, capitals, larger type, or contrasting type. Conspicuousness is a question for the court.
It must stand out.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Conspicuous

q: Ernie contracts to buy a specific antique carousel horse from Bert. At contracting, both know the horse is stored in a warehouse in another city. The contract says nothing about the place of delivery. Where is delivery due?
o: At Bert's place of business, the general default.
At the warehouse where the horse is stored.
Wherever Ernie reasonably designates.
At Ernie's home, since he is the buyer.
None of the above.
oe: That's the general default, but there's a special rule for identified goods known to be elsewhere.
Correct. § 2-308(b): for identified goods that both parties know at contracting are somewhere else, that place is the place of delivery.
The buyer doesn't choose.
The default rules never make the buyer's location the delivery place.
B is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Place of delivery: identified goods elsewhere

q: When Kermit picks up his new piano, the dealer tells him: "This piano will hold its tuning for at least a year." Kermit had already signed the contract and paid. Can the statement be an express warranty?
o: No, because Kermit gave no new consideration for it.
No, because it was made after the contract was formed.
No, because the clerk had no authority to warrant.
Yes, as a modification of the deal that needs no consideration.
Yes, but the dealer must later put it in writing.
oe: A modification needs no consideration (§ 2-209(1)).
Post-sale statements can be warranties.
Agency law supplements the Code (§ 1-103(b)), so a sales employee's statements can bind the seller.
Correct. § 2-313 cmt. 7.
Oral statements can be warranties.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Post-sale statements

q: A diner buys a sandwich at Swedish Chef's café and is injured by a piece of glass in it. Does the diner have a merchantability claim?
o: Only if the diner proves the café was negligent in preparing the sandwich.
No, because serving food is a service, not a sale.
Yes, because a sandwich with glass in it is not fit for ordinary use.
No, because the café had no way of knowing about the glass.
None of the above.
oe: Negligence is not required.
§ 2-314(1) treats serving food or drink for value as a sale.
Correct. Glass is foreign under any test.
Merchantability is strict liability.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Food served for value

q: An indefinite supply contract says: "Either party may terminate at any time without notice." Is the waiver of notice enforceable?
o: Only if both parties are merchants.
No, because reasonable notice of termination can't be waived.
Yes, because parties may vary the Code's rules by agreement.
Yes, unless its operation would be unconscionable.
Only if it is conspicuous.
oe: The test is unconscionability, not merchant status.
It can be waived unless unconscionable.
§ 2-309(3) limits this particular agreement.
Conspicuousness is not the test.
topic: 14 · Termination — Waiver of notice

q: Big Bird contracts to buy a specific antique clock from Snuffy's Antiques, a dealer. Before Big Bird picks it up, lightning destroys the shop and the clock. Who bears the loss, and what happens to the contract?
o: Big Bird must pay, because he signed the contract.
Snuffy is liable for breach, because risk had not passed.
The contract is avoided, and Snuffy bears the loss.
Snuffy must find and deliver a similar clock.
None of the above.
oe: Risk hadn't passed; a merchant seller keeps it until receipt.
The loss was without fault, so the contract is avoided.
Correct. § 2-613(a): identified goods destroyed without fault before risk passes.
The clock was unique and identified at contracting.
C is correct.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Casualty to identified goods

q: Buyer pays a $1,000 deposit on a $2,000 sofa and then repudiates. The contract has no liquidated damages clause. Seller proves no damages. How much of the deposit can Buyer recover under § 2-718(2)?
o: $0, because a breaching buyer forfeits its deposit.
$1,000, because Seller proved no damages.
$600, because Seller may keep 20% of the price.
$500, because Seller may keep up to $500.
None of the above.
oe: A breaching buyer is entitled to restitution of the excess.
Seller may keep the statutory amount.
Correct. Seller keeps the lesser of 20% of the price ($400) or $500, so Buyer recovers $1,000 − $400 = $600.
Seller keeps the lesser of 20% of the price or $500, which here is $400.
C is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Deposit restitution

q: A contract says: "Risk of loss stays with Seller until Buyer has installed and tested the goods." The goods are destroyed after delivery but before installation. Who bears the loss?
o: Seller, but the result depends on Seller being a merchant in the goods.
Seller, because the parties' agreement controls.
Buyer, because risk passes on receipt from a merchant seller.
Buyer, because the goods had already been delivered.
None of the above.
oe: The agreement controls regardless.
That is the default rule, displaced here.
The agreement overrides the default rules.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Agreement controls

q: A seller's form says: "Our warranties extend only to the original purchaser and to no other person." The state has adopted Alternative A of § 2-318. What is the effect of the clause on a household member injured by the goods?
o: It is ineffective, because a seller cannot exclude § 2-318's coverage.
It bars the claim, because the household member is not a purchaser.
It is effective, provided the clause is conspicuous.
It is effective unless the household member was a minor.
None of the above.
oe: Correct.
The seller may not exclude or limit the operation of § 2-318.
Conspicuousness doesn't help; the coverage can't be excluded.
There is no such exception.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Excluding § 2-318

q: Does the parol evidence rule apply to a tentative draft that the parties never treated as final?
o: No, unless the draft contains a merger clause.
Yes, as long as both parties signed the draft.
No, because the rule applies only to a writing intended as final.
Yes, because the rule applies to any writing the parties exchanged.
None of the above.
oe: A merger clause in a draft doesn't make it final.
A signature alone doesn't make it final.
Correct.
Only to a final expression.
C is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Unfinished draft

q: Wembley agrees to supply pipe fittings to the town "until the Doozer Tower is completed." The tower is completed. Must Wembley's customer give notice to end the deal?
o: No, because the deal ended on an agreed event.
Only if Wembley asks for notice in writing.
Yes, 30 days' written notice under § 2-309.
No, because the contract was void for indefiniteness.
Yes, because termination requires reasonable notification.
oe: The rule doesn't depend on a request.
There is no 30-day rule.
A contract ending on an agreed event is not indefinite.
Not when the contract ends on an agreed event.
topic: 14 · Termination — Agreed event

q: Kermit's purchase order offers to buy 200 chairs from Fozzie's Furniture. Fozzie's acknowledgment accepts and adds: "Interest of 1.5% per month on overdue invoices." Both are merchants, Kermit's order did not limit acceptance to its terms, and Kermit never objects. Is the interest term part of the contract?
o: No, because the term materially alters the contract.
Yes, because the acknowledgment was the last form sent.
No, because Kermit did not sign the acknowledgment.
No, because additional terms in an acceptance are mere proposals.
Yes, because it is a non-material additional term and no one objected.
oe: Interest on overdue invoices is listed in cmt. 5 as not material.
The last-shot rule is gone. The term comes in only because § 2-207(2)'s conditions are met.
§ 2-207(2) does not require the offeror's signature.
That is the rule only when one of the parties is not a merchant.

Correct. § 2-207(2): between merchants an additional term becomes part of the contract unless the offer limits acceptance, the term materially alters, or objection is given. Interest on overdue invoices is a standard example of a non-material term (cmt. 5).
topic: 2 · Formation — Additional terms between merchants

q: A signed record calls for 100 units at $1,000 total. The parties later orally agree to increase the order to 110 units at the same total price. How many units are enforceable?
o: 110, because a modification needs no consideration.
110, because the oral agreement created a course of performance.
None, because the oral modification voids the record.
110, provided the buyer has already paid.
None of the above.
oe: The statute of frauds still limits enforcement to the quantity in a record.
A single oral agreement is not a course of performance, and a course of performance can't get around the statute of frauds' quantity limit.
The original record still supports 100 units.
Payment and acceptance can help under § 2-201(3)(c), but only as to goods paid for and accepted.
Correct. Only 100 units are enforceable, because the contract is not enforceable beyond the quantity shown in the record (§ 2-201(1); Problem 3-4(c)).
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Modification and SOF: more quantity

q: A buyer's purchase order says nothing about warranties. The merchant seller's acknowledgment accepts and adds a conspicuous merchantability disclaimer. Is the disclaimer part of the contract?
o: No, because a disclaimer must be signed by the buyer to be effective.
Usually not, because a disclaimer materially alters the contract.
Yes, because it is conspicuous and mentions merchantability.
Yes, because the seller's acknowledgment was the last form sent.
None of the above.
oe: No buyer signature is required (§ 2-316(2)). The problem is § 2-207.
Correct.
First ask whether the disclaimer is part of the contract.
The last-shot rule is gone.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Disclaimer in later form

q: Under § 2-104(1), which of the following would NOT make a seller a "merchant"?
o: The seller deals in goods of the kind.
The seller once made a single sale of goods of that kind.
The seller by occupation holds itself out as having knowledge or skill about the goods.
Knowledge or skill is attributed to the seller because it employs an agent or broker who holds itself out as having that skill.
None of the above.
oe: That makes it a merchant.
Correct. An isolated sale doesn't make a seller a merchant.
That makes it a merchant (for general purposes).
That makes it a merchant.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Merchant: holding out skill

q: Prairie Dawn buys an air conditioner. The owner's manual in the box, which she reads only after installation, says the unit "is free from defects in materials and workmanship for one year." Is this statement likely part of the basis of the bargain?
o: No, because she did not read it until after the sale.
No, because she didn't negotiate any of the manual's terms.
Likely not, because it promises future performance rather than describing the unit.
Yes, because manuals and package inserts can be warranties.
None of the above.
oe: Owner's manuals and package inserts can count even if read after the sale.
Negotiation isn't required.
Express warranties can promise future performance.
Correct. Compare Problem 3-7, where the owner's manual "free of defects for one year" was likely a warranty.
D is correct.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Owner's manual

q: Big Bird gives Snuffy a new bicycle as a birthday present. The bicycle turns out to be defective. Which law governs Snuffy's rights against Big Bird?
o: UCC Article 2, because "purchase" includes a gift.
UCC Article 2, because a bicycle is a good.
UCC Article 9, because title to the bicycle passed.
The common law, because a gift is not a sale.
The law of wills, because the gift was gratuitous.
oe: "Purchase" includes a gift (§ 1-201(b)(29)) for purposes such as § 2-403, but Article 2 governs sales, which require a price.
The type of property is only the first factor. The nature of the rights transferred matters too, and a gift is not a sale.
Article 9 governs security interests.
Correct. On the class chart, a gift of goods is governed by the common law.
The law of wills governs bequests and devises.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Gift of goods

q: A buyer rejects goods that conform to the contract, giving seasonable notice. Which statement is correct?
o: The rejection is ineffective, so the buyer has accepted.
The rejection is rightful because notice was seasonable.
The seller must take the goods back and refund the price.
The rejection is effective but wrongful, so the buyer is in breach.
None of the above.
oe: A rejection can be effective even if wrongful.
Rightful rejection requires nonconforming goods.
The seller can pursue its remedies.
Correct. Effective vs. rightful rejection; § 2-703.
D is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Wrongful but effective rejection

q: Unless otherwise agreed, under § 2-307, how must the seller deliver the goods?
o: In installments as the goods become available.
In whatever lots the buyer reasonably requests.
Only after the buyer pays the price in advance.
Within 10 days after the contract is signed.
In a single delivery, with payment due on tender.
oe: The default is a single delivery.
The buyer can't require partial deliveries.
No prepayment is presumed. Payment is due on tender (§§ 2-307, 2-310(a)).
Time is a reasonable time (§ 2-309).
Correct. § 2-307.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Single delivery

q: A buyer orally agrees to buy a $200,000 sailboat, books a survey, and rents a boat slip. The seller, who never signed anything, sells to someone else. Under Casazza v. Kiser, can the buyer use promissory estoppel to enforce the oral contract?
o: No, because the buyer's reliance did not make the refusal a fraud.
Yes, because the buyer reasonably relied on the seller's promise.
No, because promissory estoppel does not apply to sales of goods.
Yes, because promissory estoppel overrides § 2-201.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The court held that promissory estoppel couldn't get around § 2-201 on these facts under any test.
Ordinary reliance was not enough.
The court analyzed the claim; it held only that this reliance wasn't enough.
Casazza held the claim failed under any test.
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Promissory estoppel and § 2-201

q: A specific painting identified at contracting is water-damaged without fault before risk passes. Under § 2-613(b), what may the buyer do?
o: Accept the painting, but at the full contract price.
Only avoid the contract and recover any deposit.
Avoid the contract or accept it with a price allowance.
Demand that the seller deliver a different painting.
Sue for damages for the water damage to the painting.
oe: The buyer may get a price allowance.
The buyer has two options.
Correct. § 2-613(b); Problem 6-6(d).
The goods were identified; there's nothing to substitute.
Accepting with an allowance waives further claims.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Partial loss

q: Which of the following is NOT required for an implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose?
o: The buyer actually relies on the seller's skill or judgment.
The seller has reason to know the particular purpose for which the goods are required.
The buyer has a particular purpose, not just the ordinary one.
The seller has reason to know the buyer is relying on the seller's skill or judgment.
The seller is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind.
oe: Required.
Required (§ 2-315).
Required (cmt. 2).
Required.
Correct. § 2-315 applies to any seller, though in practice it is usually a merchant.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Fitness: elements

q: A car dealer tells a buyer that a model is "the safest car in its class." Independent crash ratings later show it is in the middle of its class. Which statement best describes how courts treat the dealer's statement?
o: Courts split: some call it puffing, others a measurable warranty.
It is puffing, because superlatives are statements of opinion.
It is a warranty when it appears in the written contract.
It is a warranty, because a merchant dealer made it about safety.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Problem 3-6 treats it as a split: superlative puffery vs. a claim that can be checked.
Some courts would call it puffing, but not all.
Writing isn't decisive.
Merchant status doesn't decide it, and courts split.
A is correct.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Superlatives

q: A writing is a final but partial integration. The buyer offers a separate written agreement, signed at the same time, that contradicts a term. Under the class chart, is it admissible?
o: Yes, because a contemporaneous writing is part of the record.
No, because a partial integration bars contradictory terms.
Yes, but the main writing must be ambiguous on that term.
No, because it contradicts a term of a final writing.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under the Problem 5-10 chart, a contradictory contemporaneous writing is admissible against a partial integration.
Contemporaneous writings are treated as part of the record, so the bar doesn't reach them.
Ambiguity isn't required.
Under the class chart, a contemporaneous writing is part of the record, so the bar doesn't apply.
A is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Contemporaneous written

q: A fisherman buys an engine from a marine dealer. When it is delivered, the delivery receipt he signs has a merchantability disclaimer printed on the back. Is the disclaimer likely part of the contract?
o: Yes, because it mentions merchantability by name.
Yes, because he signed the receipt that contained it.
No, because it came after the contract was already formed.
No, because merchantability can't be disclaimed for marine engines.
None of the above.
oe: Mentioning merchantability matters only once the term is part of the deal.
Signing a post-sale receipt doesn't necessarily add terms.
Correct. Problem 5-4. It would have to come in as a modification (§ 2-209) or an additional term (§ 2-207).
There's no such rule.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Post-sale receipt

q: A signed record calls for delivery of 100 units on June 1. The parties later orally agree to move delivery to July 1. There is no no-oral-modification clause. Does the statute of frauds bar the modification?
o: Yes, because any change to a written contract must be in writing.
Yes, because the contract as modified is for $500 or more.
No, because § 2-209 exempts modifications from the statute of frauds.
No, because the quantity term did not change.
None of the above.
oe: That would be true only with a NOM clause, and there isn't one.
The record already satisfies § 2-201. Only the quantity must appear in it.
§ 2-209(3) says they are when the modified contract is within § 2-201.
Correct. Problem 3-4(e). A NOM clause would be a separate barrier.
D is correct.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Delivery date: no SOF problem

q: Abby takes home a painting "on approval" for a week. During that week, a fire destroys it through no fault of hers. Who bears the loss?
o: Abby, because she had possession of the painting.
The seller, but only if Abby notified it of the fire within 10 days.
Abby, because she hadn't returned it.
It is shared equally between Abby and the seller.
None of the above.
oe: In a sale on approval, risk stays with the seller.
There is no notice condition. Risk simply stays with the seller until Abby accepts.
She had a week to decide.
No splitting.
Correct. In a sale on approval, risk of loss doesn't pass to the buyer until she accepts (§ 2-327(1)(a)), so the seller bears the loss, without conditions.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Sale on approval

q: A grocery chain rightfully rejects a truckload of strawberries. The seller has no agent nearby and gives no instructions. The strawberries will spoil in two days. What should the grocery chain do?
o: Make reasonable efforts to sell them for the seller's account.
Ship them back to the seller at its own expense.
Keep them as compensation for the seller's breach.
Let them spoil, since title and risk both remain with the seller.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-603(1): a merchant buyer must follow reasonable instructions and, absent instructions, make reasonable efforts to sell perishables.
The buyer has no such duty.
The buyer may not keep them as its own.
A merchant buyer has duties with perishables.
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Merchant buyer: perishables

q: An art dealer contracts to sell a Picasso etching. Overnight, before pickup, the dealer's neglected coffee pot starts a fire that destroys it. Is the dealer excused under § 2-613?
o: No, because § 2-613 applies only to fungible goods.
No, because negligence counts as fault, so the dealer breaches.
Yes, because the etching was identified when the contract was made.
Yes, because risk hadn't passed to the buyer.
Yes, unless the buyer had paid in advance.
oe: Backwards: § 2-613 applies only to goods identified at contracting.
Correct. Problem 6-6(a). Lightning would be a different story.
The loss must also be without fault.
Risk not passing is necessary, not sufficient.
Payment doesn't affect excuse.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Negligence is fault

q: A contract says: "Seller will repair or replace defective parts." It doesn't say this is the exclusive remedy. The machine is defective. May Buyer sue for damages instead?
o: Yes, though the suit is limited to personal injuries the defect caused.
Yes, because the remedy is not expressly exclusive.
No, because the parties agreed on repair or replace.
No, because repair-or-replace clauses are exclusive by nature.
None of the above.
oe: The remedy is optional for all claims.
An agreed remedy is optional unless expressly exclusive.
They must be expressly exclusive.
B is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Limited remedy: exclusive?

q: A contract is terminated under a power in the agreement. Before termination, the buyer had failed to pay for one shipment. What happens to the seller's claim for that shipment?
o: It becomes a claim for cancellation instead.
It survives, because termination discharges only executory obligations.
It is lost unless the seller reserved it in writing.
It is discharged along with the rest of the contract.
It is reduced to the value of the goods delivered.
oe: Termination and cancellation are different events.
No reservation is needed.
Rights based on prior breach survive.
Nothing in § 2-106 reduces it.
topic: 14 · Termination — Effect of termination

q: Fozzie agrees to buy from Kermit "all the rubber chickens Fozzie requires" for his comedy shop. No estimate is stated.
