A recession hits, Fozzie's sales collapse, and his orders drop from 1,000 a month to 100. Kermit sues. Under the approach most courts take to decreases, what is the most likely result?
o: Fozzie wins, because a requirements buyer may order any amount it chooses.
Fozzie wins if the drop reflects a genuine lack of demand.
Kermit wins, because requirements contracts lack mutuality.
Kermit wins, because Fozzie must buy at least his prior average.
None of the above.
oe: Good faith limits the buyer.
Correct. § 2-306(1) measures quantity by actual requirements occurring in good faith. A genuine lack of orders can be good faith. (Some courts also apply the disproportion test to decreases.)
Requirements contracts are enforceable; the buyer's good-faith obligation supplies mutuality.
A requirements buyer isn't bound to its prior average; the quantity is its actual good-faith requirements.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Requirements: decrease in good faith

q: Kermit "sells" his delivery van to Fozzie Finance for $10,000. The agreement requires Kermit to buy the van back in one year for $11,500, and Kermit keeps using the van in his business the whole time. Which law most likely governs?
o: UCC Article 2, because the agreement expressly calls the transaction a sale.
The common law, because vans are titled under state law.
UCC Article 2A, because Kermit keeps using the van.
UCC Article 9, because the transaction is in substance a secured loan.
None of the above.
oe: Labels do not control. A "sale" with a mandatory repurchase at a higher price is in substance a loan.
Certificate-of-title rules do not change the nature of the transaction.
This is not a true lease either. Kermit is the borrower and the van secures repayment.
Correct. A sale with a mandatory repurchase at a higher price is a disguised security interest, governed by Article 9, not Article 2 (§ 2-102(3)(a)).
D is correct.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Disguised security interest

q: Grover's purchase order offers to buy 50 printers from Elmo's Electronics. Elmo's acknowledgment accepts and adds, in bold capitals: "SELLER DISCLAIMS THE IMPLIED WARRANTY OF MERCHANTABILITY." Both are merchants, and Grover never responds. Is the disclaimer part of the contract?
o: No, because Grover never signed the acknowledgment.
Yes, because it was conspicuous and specifically named merchantability.
No, because a warranty disclaimer materially alters the contract.
Yes, because Grover did not object within 10 days.
None of the above.
oe: § 2-207 doesn't require the offeror's signature. The term fails because it is material.
Conspicuousness matters under § 2-316, but first the term must get into the contract under § 2-207.
Correct. § 2-207(2)(b) and cmt. 4: a clause negating standard warranties is a classic material alteration, so it does not become part of the contract even between merchants.
The 10-day objection period belongs to the merchant's confirmation exception to the statute of frauds (§ 2-201(2)).
C is correct.
topic: 2 · Formation — Material alteration: disclaimer

q: A seller produces a signed record that satisfies § 2-201(1). What is the effect?
o: The contract is enforceable for any quantity the seller proves.
The buyer is barred from denying that a contract was formed.
The seller wins its claim unless the buyer proves a defense.
The seller may proceed but must still prove the contract and its terms.
None of the above.
oe: Enforcement stops at the quantity shown in the record.
The buyer can still deny formation and contest the terms.
The statute of frauds says nothing about whether the contract was made or breached.
Correct. Satisfying the statute of frauds only opens the courthouse door.
D is correct.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Satisfying the SOF

q: Snuffy, a farmer, contracts to sell Big Bird 100 bushels of wheat. Snuffy calls Big Bird: "The wheat is ready. Pick it up within two hours or I sell it to someone else." Is this a proper tender?
o: No, because a tender of goods must be made in writing.
Yes, because tender may be made at any time the goods are ready.
Probably not, because two hours is too short a time to hold them.
Yes, because Snuffy put the goods at Big Bird's disposition.
None of the above.
oe: Tender requires notice reasonably necessary to take delivery, not a writing.
Tender must be at a reasonable hour and for a reasonable period.
Correct. Problem 4-4. § 2-503(1)(a).
The goods must also be kept available for the period reasonably necessary for the buyer to take possession.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Tender: reasonable period

q: Kermit tells a hardware store clerk he needs paint for a boat hull, but insists on buying "BrandX Deluxe" interior paint because his cousin recommended it. The paint peels in salt water. Does Kermit have a fitness-for-purpose claim?
o: Yes, because the clerk knew Kermit's particular purpose.
Yes, because the paint failed when used for the stated purpose.
Yes, because the store is a merchant that sells paint.
No, because the paint was fit for its ordinary purpose.
No, because Kermit relied on his cousin, not on the seller.
oe: Knowledge of the purpose is not enough; the buyer must rely on the seller.
Failure alone doesn't establish a fitness warranty. The missing element is Kermit's reliance on the seller.
Merchant status is not the issue.
That is the merchantability question; it does not answer the fitness question.
Correct. There is no reliance when the buyer gives precise specifications or insists on a brand.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Fitness: brand insistence

q: A contract's exclusive remedy is repair or replacement. The seller tries to repair the machine eight times, and it still doesn't work. What happens?
o: Buyer must keep allowing repairs, since it agreed to that exclusive remedy.
The contract is void for failure of consideration.
The remedy fails of its essential purpose, and other remedies return.
Buyer may recover only a refund of the purchase price.
None of the above.
oe: Not when the remedy fails.
The remedy fails, not the contract.
The general remedies return.
C is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Failure of essential purpose

q: An art dealer sells a specific etching. Before delivery, the true owner proves it was stolen and reclaims it. Is the dealer excused under § 2-613?
o: No, but the result would change if the buyer had not yet paid.
Yes, because theft is an act of a third party.
No, because a title failure is not a casualty to the goods.
Yes, because the dealer didn't know it was stolen.
Yes, because the goods were lost without fault before risk passed.
oe: Payment doesn't matter.
The theft happened before the sale; the dealer simply had no title to sell.
Correct. Problem 6-6(b).
The warranty of title doesn't depend on knowledge.
Losing the goods to the true owner isn't a casualty.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Title failure

q: A South Dakota seller contracts to sell custom windows "properly crated … and delivered to" the buyer's construction site in New York. The windows are properly crated, but the carrier's truck crashes and they are destroyed. Who bears the loss?
o: The seller, because "delivered to" makes it a destination contract.
The carrier, as between the buyer and the seller.
The seller, because the windows were custom-made for the buyer.
The buyer, because risk passed when the carrier took the goods.
None of the above.
oe: "Delivered to" does not overcome the shipment-contract presumption.
The buyer can sue the carrier, but as between buyer and seller, the buyer bears the risk.
Custom goods don't change the risk rules.
Correct. Problem 4-7(a), based on Windows v. Jordan Panel. The buyer must look to the carrier or its insurer.
D is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Windows v. Jordan Panel

q: Which statement about the records used to satisfy § 2-201 is most accurate?
o: An unsigned writing satisfies the rule if both parties drafted it.
Only one document may be used, and it must contain every term.
Email can't satisfy the rule unless it bears a handwritten signature.
Connected writings may be read together if a signed one links them.
None of the above.
oe: The record must be signed by the party against whom enforcement is sought.
Several papers may be read together if they are connected.
A record includes email, and a typed name is a signature.
Correct. In Casazza, the signed license could not be read with the unsigned typed terms because it never referred to the boat sale.
D is correct.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Several writings

q: A contract requires monthly deliveries "by the 5th." For three months the buyer accepts deliveries on the 10th without complaint. The buyer then writes: "Going forward, we require delivery by the 5th as the contract states." The seller has not changed position in reliance. Must the seller deliver by the 5th from now on?
o: Yes, but the buyer must pay a fee for the change.
No, because the course of performance permanently modified the contract.
No, because the buyer waived the delivery term permanently.
No, because a waiver can be retracted only with new consideration.
Yes, because the buyer retracted its waiver by reasonable notice.
oe: No consideration is needed to retract a waiver.
Even if a course of performance supports waiver, the express term controls going forward once the waiver is retracted.
A waiver of an executory term can be retracted.
No consideration is needed. § 2-209(5) requires only reasonable notification, absent a material change of position in reliance.
Correct. § 2-209(5). Retraction fails only if it would be unjust because of a material change of position in reliance.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Waiver retraction

q: Which of the following is NOT barred by the parol evidence rule?
o: A prior oral agreement contradicting a term in a final writing.
A prior oral consistent term, when the writing is complete and exclusive.
A contemporaneous oral agreement contradicting a term in a final writing.
Evidence of an oral condition precedent to the contract's effectiveness.
None of the above.
oe: Barred by § 2-202.
Barred by § 2-202(b).
Barred by § 2-202.
Correct. The PER doesn't apply to conditions precedent.
D is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Condition precedent

q: Under § 1-302(b), which of the following may NOT be disclaimed by agreement?
o: The obligation of good faith.
The implied warranty of merchantability.
The place of delivery.
The time for payment.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Good faith, diligence, reasonableness, and care can't be disclaimed, though parties may set standards that aren't manifestly unreasonable.
It can be disclaimed under § 2-316.
Parties may vary the default.
Parties may vary the default.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Good faith can't be disclaimed

q: Under § 2-511, a buyer tenders payment by personal check. Which statement is correct?
o: The seller must accept a check unless the contract says otherwise.
The seller may refuse delivery without giving the buyer time to get cash.
Payment by check is conditional and fails if the check bounces.
A check is absolute payment once the seller accepts it.
None of the above.
oe: The seller may demand legal tender.
The seller must give an extension reasonably necessary to procure legal tender.
Correct. § 2-511(2)–(3). The seller may also demand legal tender, but must give the buyer a reasonable time to get it.
It is conditional.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Check payment

q: Abby, a consumer, emails a lighting store an offer to buy a lamp. The store's email reply accepts and adds a term requiring all disputes to be arbitrated. Abby never responds. Is the arbitration clause part of the contract?
o: Yes, because the store is a merchant and the term isn't material.
No, because Abby isn't a merchant, so the term is only a proposal.
Yes, because Abby's silence is acceptance of the term.
No, because the store's reply is a counteroffer Abby never accepted.
None of the above.
oe: The § 2-207(2) rule that lets additional terms in applies only "between merchants."
Correct. § 2-207(2): additional terms are proposals, and between a merchant and a consumer they become part of the contract only if the consumer agrees.
Silence does not accept a proposal.
A definite and seasonable expression of acceptance is an acceptance even with additional terms (§ 2-207(1)).
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Formation — Non-merchant: proposals

q: Count is worried that his supplier won't deliver. He calls the supplier and demands assurance. The supplier ignores the call, and Count suspends payment. Was Count entitled to suspend under § 2-609?
o: No, because § 2-609 is triggered only by a written demand.
Yes, because the supplier didn't answer within 10 days.
Yes, because he had reasonable grounds for insecurity.
No, because only a seller may demand assurance.
Yes, because any demand, oral or written, triggers § 2-609.
oe: Correct. § 2-609(1) requires the demand to be in a record (writing or electronic). Without one, there is no right to suspend.
There is no 10-day rule; and the oral demand didn't trigger § 2-609.
Grounds alone aren't enough; the demand must be in writing.
Either party may.
The demand must be in a record.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Demand in writing

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the factors used to decide which law governs a transaction?
o: The location of the parties.
Whether the parties are merchants.
The type of property involved.
The parties' agreement on governing law.
The nature of the rights being transferred.
oe: This is the third factor (domestic or international, which can bring in the CISG).
Correct. Merchant status changes particular Article 2 rules, but never whether Article 2 applies (Problem 1-4).
This is the first factor (goods, real estate, services, intellectual property).
This is the fourth factor.
This is the second factor (sale, lease, license, lien, gift).
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Four factors

q: Why is a requirements contract enforceable under the UCC even though no fixed quantity is stated?
o: Because the buyer's good-faith requirements measure the quantity.
Because the parties must state a maximum quantity.
Because the seller may decide in good faith how much to deliver.
It isn't; requirements contracts are void for indefiniteness.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-306(1): quantity is the buyer's actual requirements occurring in good faith, limited by the "unreasonably disproportionate" rule. The good-faith obligation supplies mutuality.
No maximum is needed.
The buyer's requirements set the quantity.
§ 2-306 makes them enforceable.
A is correct.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Requirements: not void for indefiniteness

q: Seller arrives at Buyer's farm on time with a truckload of wheat, but Buyer's bins aren't ready, so Seller can't unload. What is the legal effect?
o: Seller has failed to tender and is in breach.
Seller's tender is proper, and Buyer's delay excuses Seller's.
Buyer may reject the wheat, since it wasn't unloaded.
The contract is avoided, because neither party is at fault for the delay.
None of the above.
oe: Seller did everything required.
Correct. Problem 4-4. Buyer must furnish facilities reasonably suited to receiving the goods, and § 2-311(3) excuses the other party's delay.
The wheat conforms; nothing justifies rejection.
Nothing excuses performance entirely.
B is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Buyer's facilities

q: Which advertising claim is most likely an affirmation of fact rather than puffing?
o: "20,679 physicians say this brand is less irritating."
"It's toasted."
"America's favorite way to relax after a long day."
"The smoothest, mildest smoke you'll ever enjoy."
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The tobacco slides treat specific claims like this, or "immediate relief in cases of asthma," as looking like facts.
The slides treat this as puffery.
General praise.
General, unmeasurable praise.
A is correct.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Tobacco ads

q: A dealer contracts to sell "a print from the limited edition." Print #10, which the dealer meant to deliver, is water-damaged. The dealer still has print #12, which is identical. Must the dealer deliver #12?
o: Yes, but the buyer must pay extra for the substitute print.
No, because #10 was damaged without the dealer's fault.
No, because the buyer must accept #10 with an allowance.
No, because the casualty avoided the contract.
Yes, unless the contract was for print #10 specifically.
oe: The price doesn't change.
Only if the contract was for #10 specifically.
That option exists only if #10 was identified at contracting.
Avoidance requires identified goods.
Correct. Problem 6-6(c). § 2-613 applies only to goods identified when the contract was made, so if the prints are interchangeable, the dealer must deliver #12.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Interchangeable prints

q: A seller ships goods under a shipment contract, but packages them so poorly that they are crushed in normal transit. Who bears the loss?
o: The seller, because improper shipment caused the loss.
The carrier, because the goods were crushed in its hands.
The buyer, because it accepted the shipment term.
The buyer, because risk passed when the goods were delivered to the carrier.
None of the above.
oe: The goods were crushed because of the packaging.
Not when the seller's own breach causes the loss.
The seller's improper shipment changes the result.
A is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Improper packaging causes loss

q: Under § 2-302, which of the following is true?
o: The parties may agree that § 2-302 will not apply to their contract.
Unconscionability is a question of fact for the jury.
The court may refuse enforcement, strike the clause, or limit it.
Unconscionability is judged as of the time of the breach.
All of the above.
oe: § 2-302 cannot be contracted away (§ 1-302).
The court decides it as a matter of law.
Correct. Those are the three options in § 2-302(1), and the parties may present evidence of the commercial setting.
It is judged as of the time the contract was made.
Only C is correct.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Unconscionability: who decides and when

q: Seller's form and Buyer's form each say acceptance is expressly conditional on assent to its own terms, and neither party assents. Seller ships and Buyer pays. A dispute arises over the warranty terms. What are the terms of the contract?
o: The terms a reasonable merchant would have proposed.
Seller's terms, because Seller performed first.
There is no contract, because neither party assented.
Buyer's terms, because Buyer sent the last form.
The terms on which the writings agree, plus the UCC's gap fillers.
oe: Courts use the agreed terms and the Code's gap fillers.
There is no first-performer rule.
Conduct recognizing a contract is enough under § 2-207(3).
The last-shot rule is abolished.
Correct. § 2-207(3): when the writings don't form a contract but conduct recognizes one, the contract consists of the terms the writings agree on plus supplementary terms under the UCC.
topic: 2 · Formation — § 2-207(3): conduct

q: Unless otherwise agreed, how are the seller's tender of delivery and the buyer's tender of payment related?
o: Each is a condition of the other's duty to perform.
The buyer must pay before the seller must deliver.
The seller must deliver first and extend credit.
They are independent; each must perform regardless.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. §§ 2-507(1), 2-511(1): they are concurrent conditions. The seller's tender conditions the buyer's duty to accept and pay, and the buyer's tender conditions the seller's duty to deliver.
Not by default.
No credit is presumed (§ 2-310(a)).
They are conditions.
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Concurrent conditions

q: Which of the following best illustrates a "particular purpose" under § 2-315?
o: Buying a toaster to make toast for a large family each morning.
Buying a pencil to write with at work.
Buying shoes for ordinary walking around town.
Buying shoes for mountain climbing on the store's advice.
None of the above.
oe: Ordinary purpose.
Ordinary purpose.
That is an ordinary purpose (cmt. 2).
Correct. This is Comment 2's example.
D is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Ordinary vs. particular

q: Beaker agrees to be the exclusive distributor of Honeydew Labs' safety goggles in his state. The contract says nothing about effort. What duty does § 2-306(2) impose?
o: None, because the contract is silent on effort.
Only Beaker must use best efforts to promote sales.
Both must use best efforts: Beaker to sell, Honeydew to supply.
Each party must use reasonable care, but neither must use best efforts.
None of the above.
oe: § 2-306(2) fills the gap.
The duty runs both ways.
Correct. A lawful exclusive-dealing agreement imposes best efforts on both sides unless otherwise agreed.
The standard is best efforts.
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Exclusive dealing

q: A contract says: "Buyer must notify Seller of any defect within 3 days of delivery." Is this enforceable?
o: No, because notice periods cannot be varied.
Yes, if the time is not manifestly unreasonable.
Yes, because the parties agreed to the period.
No, because the UCC requires a "reasonable time."
None of the above.
oe: They can.
Correct. § 1-302(b).
Not if manifestly unreasonable.
Parties may fix a time.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Fixing reasonable time

q: Which of the following factors points toward a statement being an express warranty rather than puffing?
o: The statement was freely volunteered by the seller.
The statement was general and couldn't be measured.
The statement was specific and answered the buyer's question.
The statement was made orally rather than in writing.
The statement was hedged with "I think" or "probably" by the seller.
oe: Volunteered statements point toward puffing; answers to the buyer's questions point toward warranty.
That points toward puffing.
Correct. Those are all warranty factors on the class chart.
Oral statements can be warranties, and writing is not decisive either way.
Hedged statements point toward puffing.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Factors for warranty vs. puffing

q: After a justified written demand for adequate assurance, when does failure to provide it become a repudiation?
o: Only when performance actually comes due.
After a reasonable time, not to exceed 30 days after receipt of the demand.
Never; the demanding party may simply suspend.
After 60 days, the outer limit for a response.
After 10 days from receipt of the demand.
oe: Failure to give assurance within the time is itself a repudiation.
Failure to respond within the time is a repudiation.
The outside limit is 30 days.
That number belongs to § 2-201(2).
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — 30 days

q: Some courts require the writing to be ambiguous before admitting explanatory evidence. Which type of explanatory evidence is admissible even without ambiguity?
o: Prior negotiations between the parties.
Contemporaneous oral statements of intent.
Prior written drafts of the contract.
Course of dealing, usage of trade, and course of performance.
None of the above.
oe: Some courts require ambiguity.
Some courts require ambiguity.
Some courts require ambiguity before admitting these to explain a term.
Correct. § 2-202 cmt. 1(c).
D is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Ambiguity

q: Under a contract for monthly deliveries, the buyer accepts one delivery that arrives a week late. What is the effect of the buyer's acceptance on its right to damages for the late delivery?
o: The buyer must reject the next delivery to preserve its claim.
It keeps its claim if it notifies the seller within a reasonable time.
The buyer waived its right to damages by accepting the delivery.
The buyer created a course of performance permitting late delivery.
None of the above.
oe: No such requirement exists.
Correct. § 2-607(2)–(3)(a); Problem 3-5(A).
Acceptance does not by itself impair any remedy for nonconformity (§ 2-607(2)).
One occasion isn't a course of performance.
B is correct.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — One late delivery

q: In Razor v. Hyundai, a car's repair-or-replace warranty failed of its essential purpose. What did the court hold about the separate exclusion of consequential damages?
o: It survives unless unconscionable, and here it was unconscionable.
It was valid, because consumers may waive consequential damages.
It automatically fell along with the failed remedy.
The exclusion was valid because it was in clear capital letters.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Razor adopted the independent approach, then found the exclusion unconscionable because the buyer couldn't see it before signing.
Consumer status cuts the other way, and the court found this exclusion unconscionable.
That's the dependent approach, which the court rejected.
Capitals don't help if the buyer couldn't see it.
A is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Razor

q: A seller tenders all 100 bushels the contract calls for. The buyer arrives with a small truck and wants to take half today and half tomorrow. Has the seller made a proper tender?
o: Yes, provided the buyer pays for all 100 bushels in advance.
No, because the buyer has a right to take the goods in installments.
No, because the seller must reasonably accommodate the buyer's truck.
Yes, because delivery is in a single lot unless otherwise agreed.
None of the above.
oe: Payment is due on tender; prepayment is not the issue.
§ 2-307 says otherwise unless the parties agree.
The buyer must furnish suitable facilities.
Correct. Problem 4-4.
D is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Single lot: buyer wants partial

q: Under UCC § 1-103(b), which of the following is true?
o: Equitable doctrines such as estoppel are displaced by Article 2.
The common law applies only if the parties expressly adopt it.
The UCC displaces all common law in transactions it governs.
The common law controls whenever it conflicts with the Code.
Principles of law and equity supplement the Code unless displaced.
oe: Equity supplements the Code under § 1-103(b). Estoppel, for example, can bar a breach claim.
The common law supplements the Code automatically, without any agreement.
Too broad. § 1-103(b) keeps the common law and equity unless a particular UCC provision displaces them.
The reverse. A UCC provision displaces the conflicting common law.
Correct. § 1-103(b) lists capacity, agency, estoppel, fraud, misrepresentation, duress, coercion, mistake, and other validating or invalidating causes.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Common law supplements the Code

q: Gobo, a consumer, signs a preprinted 12-page form to buy a refrigerator. A clause in tiny type lets the seller repossess the refrigerator if Gobo is late on any payment for any item he ever buys from the seller. Gobo had no chance to negotiate. Which statement best describes how most courts would analyze the clause under § 2-302?
o: It is enforceable, because Gobo signed the form and could have read it.
Procedural unconscionability, like tiny type, is enough by itself.
The jury decides whether the clause is unfair to Gobo.
It is unconscionable only if the refrigerator's price was also unfair.
Most courts require both procedural and substantive unconscionability.
oe: Signing doesn't defeat an unconscionability claim.
Most courts want both elements.
The court decides as a matter of law.
Price is one possible kind of substantive unfairness, not a requirement.
Correct. Some courts use a sliding scale. Here the fine print and lack of choice are procedural; the one-sided repossession term is substantive.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Procedural and substantive

q: A utility signs a requirements contract for fuel oil at a fixed price, with estimates based on what it needs to generate electricity. The market price of oil rises far above the contract price. The utility then doubles its "requirements" so it can resell the extra oil at market prices. Under Orange & Rockland v. Amerada Hess, what result?
o: The utility wins, because a requirements buyer may order any amount.
The seller wins only if it proves the utility acted in bad faith.
The seller need not supply the excess, because it is unreasonably disproportionate.
The utility wins, because it acted in complete good faith.
None of the above.
oe: § 2-306(1) caps quantity at not unreasonably disproportionate to the estimate.
Disproportion is a limit separate from good faith.
Correct. The court held the doubling was unreasonably disproportionate. A requirements buyer can't use the contract to speculate on the market.
The disproportion limit applies "even where one party acts with complete good faith."
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Orange & Rockland

q: Seller insists that Buyer pay for a delivery of lumber before Buyer can inspect it. The contract is silent on inspection and payment. Who is right?
o: Seller, because inspection is only allowed after acceptance.
Buyer, because it may inspect before paying unless otherwise agreed.
Buyer, provided the lumber turns out to be defective.
Seller, because payment is due on delivery.
None of the above.
oe: Inspection comes before acceptance.
Correct. § 2-513(1); Problem 4-5(a).
The right to inspect doesn't depend on a defect.
Payment is due on receipt, but the buyer may inspect before payment unless otherwise agreed.
B is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Inspection before payment

q: Under § 2-210, which of the following uses the terms correctly?
o: A seller assigns its right to be paid and delegates its duty to deliver.
A seller delegates its right to be paid.
A buyer assigns its duty to pay.
Rights and duties are both "assigned," because the UCC uses the terms interchangeably.
A buyer delegates its right to receive the goods.
oe: Correct. Rights are assigned; duties are delegated.
A right to payment is assigned, not delegated.
A duty to pay is delegated, not assigned.
§ 2-210 keeps them apart: subsections (1) and (6) deal with delegation, (2) and (3) with assignment.
A right to receive the goods is assigned.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Rights vs. duties

q: A contract requires the seller to deliver cargo at Pier 7. A storm destroys Pier 7, but Pier 9 is available at somewhat higher cost. What must the seller do?
o: Cancel the contract, since performance at Pier 7 is impossible.
Charge the buyer the extra cost as a condition of delivery.
Tender delivery at Pier 9, which the buyer must accept.
Nothing, because the storm excuses its performance.
Wait until Pier 7 is rebuilt, then deliver there.
oe: Cancellation isn't the remedy when a substitute exists.
§ 2-614(1) requires the substitute, not a surcharge.
A commercially reasonable substitute is available.
The substitute must be used.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Substituted performance

q: In Ingram River v. Pott Industries, the seller argued that carrying and heating heavy oil was the ordinary use of barges with heating coils. How did the court respond?
o: It held that only consumer buyers can have a particular purpose for goods.
It agreed, so no fitness warranty arose for the heating coils.
It held that a fitness warranty must be stated in writing.
It held a particular purpose need not be unique, only different enough.
None of the above.
oe: There is no such rule.
The court let the fitness warranty stand.
Fitness is implied.

Correct. A particular purpose need only be sufficiently different from the customary use. Whether the goods were "tank barges" or "heating-coil barges" was a fact question, and the finding for Ingram stood.
D is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Ingram River

q: Snuffy contracts to sell Big Bird 100 bushels of wheat at $4 a bushel. Snuffy tenders 95 bushels. Has Snuffy made a proper tender?
o: Yes, as long as Big Bird pays for 95 bushels and no more.
No, and Snuffy has lost any right to cure the shortfall.
Yes, because 95 bushels is substantial performance.
No, because the short quantity is a nonconforming tender.
Yes, because a 5% shortfall is within normal variation.
oe: The tender itself is nonconforming.
Cure may be available within the contract time (§ 2-508).
Article 2 uses perfect tender, not substantial performance, for a single-delivery contract.
Correct. Problem 4-4. § 2-307 requires a single delivery, and § 2-508 may allow Snuffy to cure.
Only variations permitted by the agreement or trade usage count, and none is stated.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Short quantity tender

q: Which statement about the Official Comments to the UCC is most accurate?
o: They are a key interpretive aid, but the text controls in a conflict.
They control over the text when the two conflict.
They may be consulted only if the statute is ambiguous and no case law exists.
They are binding law in every state that enacted the Code.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. That is the order taught in Week 1: Comments first among the aids, but the statute's text governs.
The text controls if they conflict.
They are the first aid to consult, not a last resort. A tie-breaker policy is the last resort.
The Comments are not enacted law.
A is correct.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Official Comments

q: A seller ships goods under a shipment contract. The packaging is inadequate, but the goods are destroyed when the carrier's truck is hit by a train, which would have destroyed them in any packaging. Who bears the loss?
o: It is split between them, since both share some blame.
The seller, because the packaging was inadequate for the trip.
The seller, because the seller chose the carrier and the route.
The buyer, because the packaging did not cause the loss.
None of the above.
oe: No splitting.
The packaging must have caused the loss.
Choosing a carrier doesn't put transit risk on the seller.
Correct. Even with bad packaging, there is no shift of risk unless the packaging caused the loss (Windows v. Jordan Panel; Problem 4-7(d)).
D is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Bad packaging, unrelated loss

q: Under § 2-204(3), a contract for sale does not fail for indefiniteness even though one or more terms are left open if:
o: the quantity term is left open but the price is fixed.
the contract is in a writing signed by both parties and states a price.
the parties intended to contract and there is a basis for a remedy.
the parties are both merchants in goods of the kind.
the price and delivery terms are stated.
oe: The question is intent plus a basis for a remedy. A missing quantity makes a remedy harder to give, not easier.
A writing goes to the statute of frauds, not to indefiniteness.
Correct. That is the two-part test in § 2-204(3).
Merchant status is not required.
A contract can exist with an open price (§ 2-305).
topic: 2 · Formation — Open terms

q: Which of the following sellers can make an express warranty?
o: Only a merchant who deals in goods of that kind.
Any seller, whether or not a merchant.
Only a seller who receives separate consideration for the warranty.
Only a seller who puts the warranty in writing.
Only a seller who intends to make a warranty.
oe: That limit applies to merchantability (§ 2-314), not express warranties.
Correct. § 2-313 applies to any seller.
The warranty is part of the bargain; no separate consideration is needed.
Oral statements can be warranties.
Intent is not required.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Who can make an express warranty

q: Which of the following UCC provisions may the parties vary by agreement?
o: The place of delivery (§ 2-308).
The scope of Article 2 (§ 2-102).
The rights of good-faith purchasers (§ 2-403).
Unconscionability (§ 2-302).
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Gap fillers like § 2-308 apply "unless otherwise agreed."
Can't be varied; parties can't contract into or out of Article 2's scope.
Can't be varied; the rights of third parties aren't the contracting parties' to bargain away.
Can't be varied by agreement (Problem 5-1(b)).
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Non-modifiable provisions

q: Under § 2-209(4), an attempted modification that fails to satisfy a NOM clause or the statute of frauds:
o: is void for all purposes.
binds only the party who proposed it.
automatically becomes enforceable after 10 days.
can operate as a waiver.
None of the above.
oe: § 2-209(4) gives it a second life.
That is not the rule.
There is no 10-day rule.
Correct. § 2-209(4). Under § 2-209(5), a waiver of an executory term can then be retracted unless there has been a material change of position in reliance.
D is correct.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Failed modification as waiver

q: Snuffy's buyer has always paid Snuffy on time, but Snuffy learns from the trade press that the buyer is paying its other suppliers months late. Can Snuffy have reasonable grounds for insecurity?
o: No, because trade-press reports are unverified hearsay.
No, because the buyer is current on its contract with Snuffy.
Only if the buyer admits that it can't pay its debts.
Only if the buyer is insolvent in the balance-sheet sense.
Yes, because grounds need not arise from the contract at hand.
oe: Reasonable grounds are a commercial judgment, not a rule of evidence.
Grounds need not arise from this contract.
An admission isn't required.
Insolvency isn't required.
Correct. Being late on other accounts is a classic ground (§ 2-609 cmt.).
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Grounds unrelated to this contract

q: A toaster manufacturer's warranty excludes all consequential damages. The toaster catches fire and burns the consumer buyer. Is the exclusion enforceable against the personal injury claim?
o: Yes, as long as the exclusion is conspicuous.
No, because it is prima facie unconscionable for consumer injury.
No, because consequential damages can't be excluded at all.
Yes, because consequential damages may be excluded by a clear, written term.
None of the above.
oe: Conspicuousness doesn't save it.
Commercial-loss exclusions are fine.
Not for personal injury in consumer goods.
B is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Personal injury exclusion

q: Big Bird's contract for wheat requires it to be GMO-free. Big Bird wants to hold the delivered wheat for a two-week lab test before deciding whether to accept. Is that allowed?
o: Likely not, because holding the wheat for two weeks is an acceptance.
Yes, but Big Bird must pay for the wheat first.
No, because a buyer must inspect immediately on delivery.
Yes, and the seller must pay for the lab test whatever the result.
Likely yes, if two weeks is a reasonable time and manner to inspect.
oe: Possession during a reasonable inspection is not acceptance.
Inspection comes before payment unless otherwise agreed.
Inspection must be at a reasonable time and in a reasonable manner, which may be longer.
The buyer bears inspection costs unless the goods are nonconforming and rejected (§ 2-513(2)).
Correct. Problem 4-5(b). Big Bird may hold the wheat without accepting it, and pays the test costs unless the wheat fails and is rejected. The parties would do well to agree on a testing protocol.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — GMO lab test

q: A contract has a NOM clause. The seller orally assures the buyer that a late delivery date is fine, and the buyer, relying on the assurance, delays buying elsewhere. Which doctrine is LEAST likely to help the buyer avoid the NOM clause?
o: Course of performance showing waiver.
Waiver under § 2-209(4).
Estoppel under § 1-103(b).
Modification under § 2-209(1).
None of the above.
oe: A course of performance may show waiver.
Conduct can still be a waiver despite a NOM clause (Problem 3-5(C)).
Estoppel is still possible, though weak.
Correct. The NOM clause bars an unwritten modification (§ 2-209(2)). Waiver and estoppel remain possible, though the NOM clause weakens the reasonableness of reliance.
D is correct.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Estoppel and NOM

q: A seller under a shipment contract properly delivers the goods to a carrier but forgets to notify the buyer of the shipment. The goods arrive on time and undamaged. May the buyer reject them?
o: No, because shipping defects don't justify rejection after arrival.
Yes, because the seller failed to obtain the proper documents.
No, because missed notice justifies rejection only if material delay or loss results.
Yes, because the seller failed to notify the buyer promptly.
None of the above.
oe: It can if material delay or loss results.
The seller's failure was notice, and it caused no harm.
Correct. § 2-504.
Failure to notify justifies rejection only if material delay or loss results.
C is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Seller's shipment duties

q: Under § 2-306(1), which statement about the "unreasonably disproportionate" limit is correct?
o: It applies only when the buyer acts in bad faith to exploit the market.
It allows the seller to refuse any increase over the prior year's quantity.
It applies even in good faith, measured against estimates or past needs.
It applies only when the contract states an estimate of quantity.
None of the above.
oe: Orange & Rockland held it applies even when a party acts in complete good faith.
Only unreasonably disproportionate increases.
Correct. It is a limit separate from good faith, measured against any stated estimate or, if none, against normal or comparable prior requirements.
With no estimate, quantity is measured against normal or comparable prior output or requirements.
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Disproportion: separate test

q: Which of the following best describes how a contract for the sale of goods can be formed under § 2-204?
o: Only if the moment of formation can be pinpointed.
Only if the acceptance mirrors the offer's terms in every respect.
In any manner sufficient to show agreement, including conduct.
Only by a written offer and a written acceptance.
All of the above.
oe: § 2-204(2): a contract can be found even though the moment of making is undetermined.
The mirror-image rule is gone (§ 2-207(1)).
§ 2-204(1) allows any manner sufficient to show agreement.
Only C is correct.
topic: 2 · Formation — Formation by conduct

q: A used-boat seller's brochure describes a 41-foot sailboat as "seaworthy." The boat proves unseaworthy. How do courts treat this statement?
o: It cannot be a warranty, because the boat was sold used.
It is puffing, because "seaworthy" is a general opinion.
Courts split on whether a statement like "seaworthy" is a warranty.
It is a warranty only if the buyer proves reliance.
None of the above.
oe: Used goods can carry express warranties.
Not every jurisdiction agrees; courts split.
Correct. Problem 3-6 lists "seaworthy" as a split, contrasting Keith v. Buchanan with Sessa v. Riegle. In Keith, the brochure's "seaworthy" was an express warranty and no reliance had to be shown.
Keith held no proof of reliance was needed.
C is correct.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Seaworthy

q: In Top of Iowa Cooperative v. Sime Farms, the Coop demanded that the farmer pay margins (or post a letter of credit) and sign a promise to deliver. Why was that demand not unreasonable as a matter of law?
o: Because the farmer's hedge-to-arrive contracts were illegal.
Because § 2-609 lets a party demand any assurance it wants.
Because the farmer had already missed a scheduled delivery.
Because the Coop was not required to have reasonable grounds.
Because every demand for assurance asks for more than was promised.
oe: The farmer argued that; it lost.
Demands that go too far are not adequate assurance (PDM v. Brookhaven).
The farmer kept rolling delivery; the issue was future performance.
Reasonable grounds are required; the Coop had them.

Correct. The court also held that grounds for insecurity are objective and need not come from the other party's own conduct (the inverted market, the Attorney General's statement, and the farmer's silence).
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Top of Iowa

q: Under which term does the buyer NOT have a right to inspect the goods before paying?
o: "Price due on delivery."
"F.O.B. seller's warehouse."
"C.O.D." (cash on delivery).
None of the above.
oe: Inspection before payment still applies unless otherwise agreed.
A shipping term, not a payment term.
Credit terms don't eliminate inspection.
Correct. § 2-513(3): no pre-payment inspection under C.O.D. or payment-against-documents terms.
D is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — C.O.D.

q: A government regulation bars the method of payment the parties agreed on. What may the seller do?
o: Withhold delivery until the buyer offers an equivalent payment.
Demand cash in advance as a penalty for the change.
Deliver anyway and sue for the price later.
Demand payment in whatever form it chooses.
Cancel the contract at once, because performance has become impracticable.
oe: Correct. § 2-614(2): the seller may withhold or stop delivery unless the buyer provides a means of payment that is commercially a substantial equivalent.
There's no penalty.
The seller may withhold delivery.
The buyer can offer an equivalent.
The buyer gets a chance to offer an equivalent.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Payment method fails

q: Prairie Dawn hires Speedy Print to print and bind 500 copies of her art book. Most of the price reflects Speedy Print's labor. When the books arrive with smeared pages, does Article 2 govern Prairie Dawn's claim?
o: Yes, but that is because Speedy Print is a merchant printer.
No, because most of the price is for services.
No, because hybrid transactions fall outside Article 2 altogether.
Yes, because services that manufacture goods count on the goods side.
No, because a book is intellectual property, not goods.
oe: Scope never depends on merchant status.
Services that manufacture the goods count toward the goods side of the predominance test (§ 2-102(2) cmt. 3).
Under the 2022 amendments, Article 2 applies fully to a hybrid transaction in which goods predominate, and in part even when they don't.
Correct. That is Problem 1-2. And because the claim concerns the conformity of the books, Article 2's warranty rules would apply even if services predominated.
The buyer is purchasing printed books, which are movable things, not a license of the copyright.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Hybrid: manufacturing services

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a liquidated damages clause from a remedy limitation?
o: They are tested the same way, for reasonableness.
An LD clause fixes the amount; a limitation caps categories of loss.
An LD clause must be conspicuous; a limitation need not be.
A limitation fixes the amount of damages in advance; an LD clause caps them.
None of the above.
oe: They have different tests.

Correct. Problem 5-9. An LD clause fixes damages in advance and is tested for reasonableness. A limitation caps or eliminates categories, the buyer still proves actual loss, and it is tested by failure of essential purpose or unconscionability.
Neither must be conspicuous.
Reversed. The LD clause sets the amount; a limitation caps or removes categories.
B is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — LD vs. limitation

q: Kermit contracts to sell Fozzie 100 standard steel I-beams. Kermit delegates the duty to deliver to Gonzo's Steel, which never delivers. Who is liable to Fozzie for the nondelivery?
o: Only Kermit, because Gonzo's Steel made no promise to Fozzie.
Kermit, because delegating a duty doesn't relieve the delegator.
Fozzie bears the loss, because he should have demanded assurance from Gonzo's Steel.
Only Gonzo's Steel, because Kermit delegated the duty.
No one, because Fozzie never consented to the delegation.
oe: If Gonzo's Steel accepted an assignment of "the contract," it promised to perform, and Fozzie can enforce that promise (§ 2-210(5)). Kermit is liable either way.
Correct. § 2-210(1). If Gonzo's Steel accepted an assignment of the contract, it is liable too, because its acceptance is a promise to perform that Fozzie can enforce (§ 2-210(5)).
§ 2-210(6) lets Fozzie demand assurance, but it is optional. Failing to ask doesn't cost him his claim.
Delegation never relieves the delegator.
Standard I-beams: Fozzie has no substantial interest in Kermit personally performing, so no consent was needed.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Delegator stays liable

q: Kermit emails Fozzie: "Confirming I'll buy 40 drum kits from you at $600 each. — Kermit." Kermit typed his name; there is no handwritten signature. Fozzie sues Kermit when Kermit backs out. Is the email a sufficient record signed by Kermit?
o: Yes; an email is a record, and a typed name can sign it.
No, because § 2-201 requires a handwritten signature.
Yes, provided Fozzie also signed the email reply.
No, because an email is not a writing under § 2-201.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under the 2022 amendments (and UETA elsewhere), email is a record, and a typed name adopted to authenticate it is a signature.
A typed name can be a signature.
Only the party against whom enforcement is sought (Kermit) must sign.
"Record" includes electronic records.
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Email as a signed record

q: Gonzo tells a sporting-goods dealer that he needs a tent that will survive a Himalayan blizzard, and asks the dealer to pick one. The dealer picks a summer tent. Gonzo's reliance on this dealer was arguably unreasonable because the dealer obviously knew little about mountaineering. Does that defeat a fitness claim?
o: No, because reliance must be actual but need not be reasonable.
Yes, because the dealer is no mountaineering expert.
No, because the dealer is a merchant in sporting goods.
Yes, because the buyer's reliance must be reasonable.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The outline's fitness elements: seller need not be a merchant, and reliance need not be reasonable.
The dealer had reason to know Gonzo relied on its selection.
Merchant status is not the reason.
§ 2-315 doesn't require the buyer's reliance to be reasonable, only actual.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Fitness: reasonable reliance

q: A seller who is not a merchant sells a boat engine with a written merchantability disclaimer that is not conspicuous. Does the buyer have a merchantability claim?
o: Yes, because merchantability is implied in every sale of goods.
No, because a non-merchant makes no merchantability warranty.
No, because the written disclaimer bars the claim.
Yes, because the disclaimer is not conspicuous enough to work.
None of the above.
oe: Only merchants.
Correct. Problem 5-4. Fitness can still arise if its elements are met.
A disclaimer that isn't conspicuous wouldn't work, but the claim fails anyway: no merchantability warranty arose.
First ask whether the warranty arose at all.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Non-merchant: no merchantability

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the Orange & Rockland factors for deciding whether a requirements increase is unreasonably disproportionate?
o: The size of the excess over the estimate.
The gap between the market price and the contract price.
Whether the buyer is a merchant in the goods.
The reason for the increase.
The seller's ability to foresee the increase.
oe: One of the five factors.
One of the factors.
Correct. Merchant status is not a factor. The fifth factor is whether the market rise was fortuitous.
One of the factors.
One of the factors.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Orange & Rockland factors

q: A contract between Kermit and Fozzie expressly requires delivery by noon. Over many prior contracts, Fozzie always accepted deliveries by 5 p.m., and in this industry deliveries are customarily accepted until 6 p.m. If these cannot reasonably be read together, which controls?
o: The course of dealing allowing delivery by 5 p.m.
The express term requiring delivery by noon.
The usage of trade allowing delivery by 6 p.m.
Whichever practice is most favorable to the buyer.
None of the above.
oe: Course of dealing ranks below express terms.
Correct. § 1-303(e): express terms prevail over course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade.
Usage of trade ranks last.
There is no pro-buyer tie-breaker.
B is correct.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Hierarchy

q: Which of the following is a way UCC Article 2 changed the common-law rules of offer and acceptance?
o: An acceptance may be made in any reasonable manner and medium.
A merchant's signed offer can be irrevocable without consideration.
An acceptance need not mirror the offer to form a contract.
An order for prompt shipment can be accepted by shipping the goods.
All of the above.
oe: True (§ 2-206(1)(a)), but it is not the only change listed.
True (§ 2-205), but not the only change.
True (§ 2-207(1)), but not the only change.
True (§ 2-206(1)(b)), but not the only change.
Correct. The slides list all four, plus treating a written confirmation as an acceptance (§ 2-207(1)).
topic: 2 · Formation — How the UCC changed offer and acceptance

q: Miss Piggy commissions the famous painter Lew Zealand to paint her portrait, to be delivered framed. Lew delegates the job to one of his students. Must Miss Piggy accept the student's portrait?
o: No, because she has a substantial interest in Lew's own work.
Yes, because duties under Article 2 are freely delegable.
Yes, as long as the student is just as skilled a painter.
Yes, because Lew remains liable if the portrait is bad.
No, because a portrait is a service, so Article 2 doesn't apply.
oe: Correct. § 2-210(1). A portrait by a famous artist is the classic case of a personal performance.
Not when the other party has a substantial interest in having the original promisor perform.
The question is Miss Piggy's interest in Lew's performance, not the student's skill.
Lew would remain liable, but that doesn't force Miss Piggy to accept a substitute performance she has a substantial interest in avoiding.
A painting is a good, and § 2-210 governs the delegation.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Substantial interest

q: Rosita picks out a specific used piano at Rowlf's music shop and signs a contract to buy it. Rowlf will deliver it next month after tuning it. When is the piano identified to the contract?
o: When Rowlf first priced the piano for sale.
When the piano is loaded onto Rowlf's truck.
When Rosita pays the full price.
When the contract is made.
When Rowlf tenders the piano.
oe: The goods must be identified to this contract, which hadn't been made yet.
Identification happened earlier, at contracting.
Payment doesn't control identification.
Correct. § 2-501(1)(a): if the contract is for existing goods already identified, identification occurs when the contract is made.
Identification comes earlier.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Identification

q: A buyer agreed to pay C.O.D. When the shipment arrives, the crate is visibly smashed and leaking. Must the buyer pay before inspecting?
o: No, because the nonconformity is apparent without inspection.
Yes, but the buyer may reject the goods after paying.
Yes, because C.O.D. means the buyer must pay first.
No, because a buyer may always inspect before paying, even C.O.D.
None of the above.
oe: The buyer is excused from paying here.
§ 2-512(1)(a) has an exception.
C.O.D. normally removes the pre-payment inspection right.
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Pay before inspection

q: In PDM v. Brookhaven, PDM, while building a water-storage tank, said it would be "assured" only by a personal guarantee, escrow financing, or buying an interest in Brookhaven. How did the court treat that demand?
o: As an enforceable modification of the construction contract.
As a proper demand for adequate assurance under § 2-609.
As a waiver of PDM's right to the contract payments.
As demanding more than adequate assurance as a matter of law.
As unnecessary, because PDM had no grounds for insecurity.
oe: Brookhaven never agreed to these terms.
It went beyond adequate assurance.
Not the holding.
Correct. § 2-609 doesn't let a party redraft the contract. The casebook contrasts PDM with Top of Iowa.
The problem was the scope of the demand.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — PDM v. Brookhaven

q: Can an implied warranty be excluded by course of dealing or usage of trade?
o: Only fitness can be excluded that way, not merchantability.
Only merchantability can be excluded that way, not fitness.
Yes, by course of dealing, course of performance, or trade usage.
No, implied warranties may be excluded only by written words.
None of the above.
oe: § 2-316(3)(c) reaches all implied warranties.
§ 2-316(3)(c) reaches all implied warranties.
§ 2-316(3)(c) also allows exclusion by course of dealing, course of performance, or usage of trade.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Trade usage disclaimer

q: Oscar steals Telly's bicycle and sells it to Herry, who pays fair value and has no idea it was stolen. Telly finds the bicycle and sues Herry to get it back. Who wins?
o: Herry, because he is a good-faith purchaser for value.
Herry, because Oscar had voidable title.
Telly, provided he reported the theft to the police.
It depends on whether Herry had notice of Telly's interest.
None of the above.
oe: Good-faith purchase protects a buyer only from a seller with voidable title, not a thief.
A thief has void title, not voidable title.
Reporting the theft doesn't matter. A thief has void title whether or not the owner reported it.
Notice is irrelevant when the seller is a thief.
Correct. Telly wins because a thief has void title and passes nothing, even to a good-faith purchaser for value (§ 2-403(1)). C adds a condition the law doesn't impose.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Title: thief

q: Kermit, in Ohio, contracts to sell Fozzie, in Texas, 200 banjos. The contract says "ship to Fozzie's store in Austin." It contains no F.O.B. term and says nothing about risk of loss. Kermit properly delivers the banjos to a carrier, and they are destroyed in a highway accident. Who bears the loss?
o: Fozzie, because risk passed when Kermit delivered to the carrier.
The carrier, because it had possession when they were destroyed.
Kermit, because the banjos never reached Fozzie's store.
The loss is split equally between Kermit and Fozzie.
Kermit, because naming a destination makes it a destination contract.
oe: Correct. § 2-509(1)(a). A "ship to" term just tells the seller where to send the goods; it doesn't make the contract a destination contract.
The buyer may sue the carrier, but as between buyer and seller, Fozzie bears the risk.
That would be true only in a destination contract.
There is no splitting rule.
Naming a destination doesn't overcome the shipment-contract presumption.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Shipment contract presumption

q: Under the 2022 amendments to Article 2, if the goods in a hybrid transaction do NOT predominate, which of the following Article 2 provisions still applies?
o: The statute of frauds for sales of goods (§ 2-201).
The battle-of-the-forms rule (§ 2-207).
The implied warranty of merchantability (§ 2-314).
The rule on modifications without consideration (§ 2-209).
None of the above.
oe: Under § 2-102(2) cmt. 5, § 2-201 does not apply when goods don't predominate.
The formation rules (§§ 2-204 to 2-207) do not apply when goods don't predominate.

Correct. Provisions that relate primarily to the goods still apply, including the warranties (§§ 2-312 to 2-318), tender and risk of loss, acceptance, rejection and cure, and the buyer's remedies for nonconforming goods.
§ 2-209 does not apply when goods don't predominate.
C is correct.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Hybrid: what applies when goods don't predominate

q: What is the difference between a warranty disclaimer and a remedy limitation?
o: A disclaimer limits damages; a limitation removes the warranty.
A disclaimer means no breach; a limitation caps damages for one.
A disclaimer must be conspicuous; a limitation must be in a separate signed document.
They are the same thing, just labeled differently.
None of the above.
oe: Reversed.
Correct.
Merchantability disclaimers can be oral, and limitations need not be conspicuous or separately signed.
They work at different steps: a disclaimer goes to breach, a limitation to damages.
B is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Disclaimer vs. limitation

q: A tenant asks its landlord several times over 19 months to discuss the tenant's option to buy the building. The landlord evades every request, then declares the option void because the tenant missed a technical step. Under the note case Brunswick Hills, how would a court likely view the landlord's conduct?
o: As permitted, because the tenant should have hired a lawyer.
As bad faith, because it exploited an oversight it could have fixed.
As permitted, because good faith applies only to negotiation.
As permitted, because a party may always insist on strict compliance with the contract.
As bad faith, because a landlord owes its tenant fiduciary duties.
oe: The landlord's evasion is the problem, not the tenant's lack of counsel.
Correct. Brunswick Hills (N.J.) found bad faith in the landlord's 19 months of evasion.
Good faith applies to performance and enforcement.
Strict compliance is usually fine, but not when the party has strung the other side along to manufacture the default.
Good faith is less than a fiduciary duty.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Brunswick Hills

q: Rizzo agreed to supply cheese at a fixed price. A drought doubles the market price of milk, and the contract becomes a big loss for Rizzo. Is Rizzo excused under § 2-615?
o: Yes, because performance has become unprofitable.
Yes, because a drought is an act of God beyond Rizzo's control.
No, because § 2-615 doesn't apply to contracts for food.
No, because a rise in cost alone is not an excuse.
Yes, if the drought and price rise were unforeseeable.
oe: Increased cost alone doesn't excuse.
The question is whether performance became impracticable, not merely costlier.
There is no such limit.

Correct. § 2-615 cmt. 4: increased cost or a rise in the market alone is not an excuse. A severe shortage of raw materials due to a contingency like a crop failure that prevents performance could be different.
Even unforeseeable cost increases rarely excuse.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Increased cost

q: A sales rep tells a building owner that a new HVAC unit "puts out 300,000 BTUs per hour" and that "you'll be very happy with it." The brochure, which the owner skimmed, says the unit runs "under 100 decibels." Which statements are likely express warranties?
o: All three, because each was made to induce the sale.
None of them, because the owner didn't rely on any of them.
Only "300,000 BTUs per hour," because the owner barely read the brochure.
Only "you'll be very happy with it," because it's a promise.
The BTU and decibel statements, but not "very happy."
oe: "You'll be very happy" is puffing.
No particular reliance need be shown (§ 2-313 cmt. 3).
Skimming the brochure doesn't take its specific statement out of the basis of the bargain.
That is puffing.
Correct. Problem 3-7. Specific, measurable statements are warranties; "you'll be very happy" is puffing.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — HVAC statements

q: Under a requirements contract, Rizzo's bakery has historically ordered 90,000 to 100,000 pounds of flour a year. Rizzo honestly lands a huge new supermarket customer and orders 400,000 pounds. Which statement best describes the order?
o: It is proportionate to his needs but placed in bad faith.
It is binding on the seller, because the buyer acted in good faith.
It is both in bad faith and unreasonably disproportionate.
It may be in good faith yet unreasonably disproportionate.
None of the above.
oe: That would be a normal-size order placed to resell at a higher market price.
Good faith doesn't override the disproportion limit.
Rizzo honestly needs the flour; nothing suggests bad faith.
Correct. That is Problem 4-2's example of a good-faith but disproportionate demand.
D is correct.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Good faith but disproportionate

q: When is a buyer most likely to accept an express disclaimer of the warranty of title?
o: When the buyer is a merchant who can investigate title.
Whenever the seller is a consumer rather than a professional dealer.
When provenance is uncertain and the price reflects that risk.
When buying new goods from an authorized dealer.
None of the above.
oe: Merchant buyers get the title warranty too; what matters is uncertain provenance reflected in the price.
Consumers still make the title warranty.
Correct. Problem 5-5.
Ordinary sales carry the warranty.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Quitclaim title

q: Under the UCC, what is the difference between the "agreement" and the "contract"?
o: The agreement includes only express terms, never course of dealing or usage of trade.
The agreement must be in writing, but the contract need not be.
The agreement is the bargain in fact; the contract is the resulting legal obligation.
The contract is the parties' bargain in fact; the agreement is the legal obligation.
Nothing; the Code uses them interchangeably.
oe: The agreement includes the bargain as found in course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade.
Neither definition requires a writing.
Correct. § 1-201(b)(3) and (b)(12). The contract can include more (gap fillers, implied warranties) or less (an unconscionable term, a term barred by the statute of frauds) than the agreement.
That reverses the definitions.
The Code defines them differently.
topic: 2 · Formation — Agreement vs. contract

q: Elmo buys Grover's rare comic book with a check that bounces. Before Grover discovers the problem, Elmo sells the comic to Abby, who pays fair value in good faith. Can Grover recover the comic from Abby?
o: Yes, because a buyer who pays with a bad check is like a thief.
No, because Elmo had voidable title and Abby bought in good faith.
Yes, because Elmo never actually paid for the comic.
No, because Grover was negligent in accepting a check.
None of the above.
oe: A dishonored check gives voidable, not void, title.
Correct. § 2-403(1) lists the dishonored check as a voidable-title case.
A buyer whose check is dishonored gets voidable title.
Negligence isn't the test.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Title: voidable title

q: A buyer inspects a shipment of chairs, finds them nonconforming, and rightfully rejects them. Who bears the cost of the inspection?
o: The buyer pays at first but may recover it from the seller.
The seller, whatever the result of the inspection.
The buyer, because inspection is done for its own benefit and protection.
The carrier, if the goods were damaged in transit.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-513(2): the buyer bears inspection costs, but may recover them if the goods are nonconforming and rejected.
Only if the goods are nonconforming and rejected.
The buyer bears the cost but recovers it in this situation.
The carrier has nothing to do with inspection costs.
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Inspection costs

q: "F.O.B. buyer's location" means:
o: The seller pays the freight, but risk passes to the buyer when the goods are delivered to the carrier.
Risk passes to the buyer when the goods are delivered to the carrier.
The carrier bears the risk until the goods arrive.
The risk is shared equally until delivery.
None of the above.
oe: Half right. F.O.B. the destination puts both the expense and the risk of transit on the seller (§ 2-319(1)(b)).
That describes F.O.B. seller's location (a shipment contract).
As between seller and buyer, the seller bears the risk.
There's no sharing.

Correct. "F.O.B. buyer's location" makes a destination contract: the seller bears the expense and risk of getting the goods there, and risk passes when they are duly tendered at the buyer's location (§§ 2-319(1)(b), 2-509(1)(b)).
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — F.O.B. buyer's location

q: In a heavily negotiated deal, a buyer misses a contract deadline through its own carelessness. The seller says nothing and then relies on the missed deadline to end the deal. Under the note case Vintage Rodeo, has the seller breached the duty of good faith?
o: Yes, because the seller owed the buyer fiduciary duties.
Yes, because good faith overrides express deadlines.
No, because the seller merely benefited from the buyer's own mistake.
Yes, because good faith required the seller to warn the buyer.
No, because good faith doesn't apply between merchants.
oe: Contract parties are not fiduciaries.
Good faith can't contradict express terms.
Correct. Vintage Rodeo (Del. Ch.). Contrast Market Street, where the party actively exploited a known oversight.
Good faith is not a duty to protect the other side from its own mistakes.
It applies to everyone.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Vintage Rodeo

q: A contract between Big Bird and Snuffy's Seed Co. says: "Neither party may assign this contract." Snuffy's Seed Co. assigns to its bank the right to be paid under the contract. What is the effect of the clause?
o: It bars the assignment of the right to payment.
It bars both assignment of rights and delegation of duties.
It lets Big Bird cancel the contract for breach.
It makes the assignment to the bank void.
It bars only delegation of Snuffy's duties.
oe: A ban on assigning "the contract" is read narrowly.
Under § 2-210(4) it bars only delegation.
The assignment of a right to payment isn't a breach that would justify cancellation.
To make an assignment ineffective, a clause must say something like "any attempted assignment is void," and even that can't stop an assignment of a right to payment (§ 9-406(d)).
Correct. § 2-210(4): unless the circumstances indicate otherwise, a prohibition on assigning "the contract" bars only the delegation of performance.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — "Assign the contract" ban

q: When is specific performance most likely available to a buyer?
o: When the goods are unique or in other proper circumstances.
Whenever the buyer has already paid in full.
Never, because the UCC limits buyers to damages.
Whenever the seller's breach is willful.
Only if the seller is a merchant who deals in goods of that kind.
oe: Correct. § 2-716.
Payment doesn't matter.
It is available rarely.
Only rarely.
The seller's status isn't the test; uniqueness or other proper circumstances are.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Specific performance

q: A fire destroys half of a manufacturer's plant, and it can't supply all its customers. What does § 2-615 require of the manufacturer?
o: Allocate remaining output fairly and notify buyers seasonably.
Nothing, because the fire excuses all performance.
Supply its highest-paying customers first, then the rest.
Supply only the customers who signed most recently.
Stop all deliveries until the plant is fully rebuilt.
oe: Correct. § 2-615(b)–(c): allocate production fairly and reasonably among customers, and seasonably notify each buyer of the delay or allocation.
Partial capacity must still be allocated.
It must allocate fairly.
That isn't fair allocation.
Partial capacity must be allocated.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Allocation

q: Count's buyer pays 15 days after each delivery. Count learns the buyer's credit rating was downgraded and it changed banks. Count announces that from now on it will ship only cash on delivery. What is the risk?
o: None, because the buyer must accept COD from any seller.
None, because § 2-609 lets Count impose any new terms it chooses.
None, because a downgrade lets the seller change the credit terms.
The buyer may cancel only if Count fails to give 30 days' notice.
Changing the terms on its own may be a repudiation.
oe: Not so; COD isn't in the contract.
§ 2-609 lets Count demand assurance and suspend, not rewrite the deal.
§ 2-702(1) allows a seller to demand cash only if the buyer is insolvent.
That isn't the rule.
Correct. Problem 6-3(a). Count should instead demand adequate assurance under § 2-609.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Seller demands COD

q: Dr. Bunsen Honeydew, a scientist, sells his own used car to his lab assistant Beaker. The car's transmission fails a week later. Does Beaker have a claim for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability?
o: No, because this is not an Article 2 transaction.
No, because Bunsen is not a merchant with respect to cars.
Yes, because there is an implied promise that goods are fit for their ordinary purpose.
No, because the car is used, so it is sold as is.
None of the above.
oe: A sale of a car is an Article 2 transaction, whoever the parties are.
Correct. A scientist making an isolated sale of his own car is not a merchant who deals in cars.
That promise arises only when the seller is a merchant with respect to goods of that kind (§ 2-314(1)).
Used goods can carry the merchantability warranty; the standard is just adjusted to used goods.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Merchantability: who is a merchant

q: When does a buyer acquire an insurable interest in goods?
o: When title passes to the buyer.
When the buyer pays for the goods.
When the risk of loss passes to the buyer.
When the goods are identified to the contract.
None of the above.
oe: The buyer gets an insurable interest earlier.
Payment isn't the trigger.
The buyer's insurable interest arises earlier, on identification.
Correct. § 2-501(1). The seller keeps an insurable interest while it has title or a security interest.
D is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Insurable interest

q: Under a single one-year contract, Bert has delivered pigeon feed in 50-pound sacks every week for six months, and Ernie has accepted each delivery without objection. The contract does not say what size sacks to use. Which concept best describes this pattern?
o: Usage of trade.
Course of performance.
Course of dealing.
Modification.
Waiver.
oe: Usage of trade is an industry-wide practice, not a practice between these two parties.
Correct. Repeated occasions for performance under this contract, accepted with knowledge and an opportunity to object, form a course of performance (§ 1-303(a)).
Course of dealing is conduct in prior transactions, before this contract.
A course of performance may show a modification, but nothing here suggests the parties agreed to change a term.
A course of performance may show waiver, but the pattern itself is a course of performance.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Course of performance vs. dealing

q: A homeowner contracted with Anthony Pools to build a swimming pool. Services predominated, but the contract included a diving board, which was defective and injured the homeowner. Under the gravamen-of-the-claim test, what result?
o: Article 2 does not apply, because the predominant purpose of the contract was services.
Article 2 applies to the whole contract, including the construction work.
No warranty applies, because the homeowner is a consumer.
Article 2 applies to this claim, because it concerns the diving board.
None of the above.
oe: That is the predominant-purpose result. The gravamen test asks instead whether the claim concerns the goods.
The gravamen test sorts the claims. It applies Article 2 only to the claim about the goods.
Consumers get Article 2 warranties too.
Correct. In Anthony Pools (note case), the Maryland court applied the merchantability warranty to the unmerchantable diving board even though services predominated.
D is correct.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Gravamen test

q: Under Article 2, which statement about risk of loss is correct?
o: Risk of loss passes when the buyer signs the contract.
Risk of loss passes when the buyer pays the price.
Risk is allocated by specific rules, not by who has title.
Risk of loss follows title to the goods.
Risk stays with the seller until the buyer takes possession.
oe: Signing passes neither title nor risk by itself.
Payment doesn't control.
Correct. Risk goes to the party in control, the one likely to be insured, or the one in breach.
Article 2 separates risk of loss from title.
Not for non-merchant sellers or shipment contracts.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Risk not tied to title

q: The continuum of protection runs from freedom of contract to paternalism. Which buyer are courts most likely to protect from a warranty disclaimer?
o: A merchant buying ordinary commercial goods from another merchant.
A consumer buying prepackaged new consumer goods.
A buyer of used goods from a dealer.
A merchant buying specially made commercial goods.
None of the above.
oe: Closer to freedom of contract.
Correct. That is the paternalism end of the continuum.
In the middle.
That end is freedom of contract.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Disclaimer continuum

q: Ernie buys 500 euro notes from a currency dealer to spend on his trip to Rome. Bert buys a rare 1850 coin from a coin dealer to keep in his collection. Which of these purchases is most clearly a sale of "goods"?
o: Both purchases.
Neither purchase.
It depends entirely on whether the dealers are merchants.
Ernie's purchase only.
Bert's purchase only.
oe: The euro notes are only "depends." Currency bought as money is arguably not goods.
The collector's coin is a good.
Whether something is a good does not turn on merchant status.
Currency bought to be spent as money is the weaker case. Whether it is goods depends on whether it is bought as a commodity or as money.

Correct. The collector's coin is the subject of the sale, not the money paying the price, so it is a good (Problem 1-1). Ernie's euros are the harder case: it depends whether the currency is a commodity or money.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Money as goods

q: Wembley is an accountant. Twice a year he sells his handmade stained-glass ornaments at a craft fair, and he has done so for years. Does Wembley give the implied warranty of merchantability on the ornaments?
o: No, because he sells ornaments only twice a year.
Yes, because he regularly sells goods of that kind.
No, because his main occupation is accounting, not crafts.
No, because handmade goods carry no implied warranties.
None of the above.
oe: Regular, recurring sales are enough.
Correct. Problem 3-9. A merchant is one who deals in goods of the kind (§ 2-104(1)), and his day job is not decisive.
His occupation doesn't stop him from also dealing in ornaments.
Handmade goods are goods.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Artisan at craft fair

q: A contract says: "Any assignment of Seller's right to payment is prohibited and void." Seller assigns its right to payment to a bank anyway. Is the assignment effective?
o: No, because the contract makes it void.
Yes, but it needs Buyer's written consent first.
Yes, but Seller is in breach and owes Buyer damages.
No, unless the bank is a merchant.
None of the above.
oe: § 9-406(d) overrides the clause.
Buyer's consent isn't required.
Under § 9-406(d), making the assignment is not a breach either.
