The assignee's status doesn't matter.
Correct. The assignment is effective despite the clause, because a term barring assignment of a right to payment is ineffective, and making the assignment isn't a breach (§ 9-406(d); Problem 6-2(b)).
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — § 9-406(d)

q: A contract between a Chicago seller and a Boston buyer says "F.O.B. Chicago." The goods are damaged in transit through no fault of the seller. Who bears the loss?
o: The seller, because the goods never reached Boston.
The seller, because it chose and contracted with the carrier.
The buyer, provided it has already paid for the goods.
The buyer, because risk passed on delivery to the carrier.
None of the above.
oe: F.O.B. the seller's city is a shipment contract.
The seller's duty is to make a reasonable transport contract, not to insure the trip.
Payment is irrelevant to risk of loss.
D is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — F.O.B. seller's city

q: Which of the following is an acceptance of goods by the buyer under § 2-606?
o: Paying for the goods before inspecting them.
Inspecting the goods at the buyer's plant.
Taking possession of the goods at the buyer's plant to inspect them.
Failing to reject effectively after a chance to inspect.
All of the above.
oe: Payment is not acceptance (§ 2-512(2)).
Inspection precedes acceptance.
Possession is not acceptance.
Only D is an acceptance.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — What is acceptance

q: Elmo orally agrees to buy a used guitar from Grover for $450. Grover later refuses to deliver, claiming the contract is unenforceable because it is not in writing. Is Grover right?
o: Yes, because Grover is not a merchant who deals in guitars.
Yes, because contracts for the sale of goods must be in writing.
Yes, because the guitar is used goods sold privately.
No, because Elmo can prove the contract by his own testimony.
No, because the statute applies only at $500 or more.
oe: Merchant status does not affect the $500 threshold.
Only contracts for $500 or more fall within § 2-201(1).
Used goods are covered by the same rule.
Testimony would not get around § 2-201 if it applied. The point is that it doesn't apply.
Correct. § 2-201(1) applies only to sales for $500 or more, so at $450 the oral contract is enforceable without a record.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — $500 threshold

q: Under § 2-616, after receiving a seller's notice of allocation, a buyer says nothing for 30 days. What happens?
o: The contract is reinstated in full as originally written.
The buyer is deemed to accept the allocation.
The contract lapses with respect to the affected deliveries.
The buyer is in breach for failing to respond in time.
The seller must deliver the full contract quantity.
oe: No.
Silence for 30 days leads to lapse.
Silence isn't a breach.
The contract lapses as to the affected deliveries.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Buyer silence

q: A contract's exclusive remedy for a defective TV is "store credit." Before the buyer can use it, the retailer goes bankrupt and its stores close. What result?
o: The buyer may recover only the price it paid.
The remedy is unconscionable, so the whole contract is void.
The buyer is stuck with the credit it bargained for.
The remedy failed of its essential purpose; general remedies return.
None of the above.
oe: The general remedies return in full.
Failure of essential purpose affects the remedy, not the contract.
An exclusive remedy that fails of its essential purpose doesn't bind the buyer.
Correct. Problem 5-7 (the Circuit City example). § 2-719(2).
D is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Worthless store credit

q: Elmo obtains a guitar from Grover by fraud, giving him voidable title. Elmo then gives the guitar to Zoe as a birthday present. Zoe has no idea of the fraud. Can Grover recover the guitar from Zoe?
o: Yes, because Zoe gave no value for the guitar.
No, because Elmo had voidable title when he gave it away.
No, because Zoe received it in complete good faith.
No, because a gift counts as a "purchase" under the UCC.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. "Purchase" includes a gift (§ 1-201(b)(29)), but § 2-403(1) protects only a good-faith purchaser for value, so Zoe takes only Elmo's voidable title.
Voidable title can become good title only in the hands of a good-faith purchaser for value.
Good faith alone isn't enough; she must also give value.
A gift is a purchase, but it is not a purchase for value.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Title: gift from voidable-title holder

q: Under a contract for 12 monthly shipments, Seller ships the first installment two days late, and Buyer accepts it without objection. Has a course of performance been established that permits late delivery?
o: No, because a course of performance can arise only between merchants.
Yes, because Buyer accepted the late shipment with knowledge of the delay.
No, because a course of performance requires repeated occasions for performance.
Yes, because Buyer failed to object within 10 days.
No, because a course of performance can only arise before the contract is made.
oe: Course of performance isn't limited to merchants. The problem is that one occasion isn't enough.
Knowledge and acceptance are part of the test, but one occasion is not enough.
Correct. § 1-303(a). A single occasion isn't enough (Problem 3-5(A)).
The 10-day objection rule belongs to § 2-201(2).
That is course of dealing. Course of performance arises after contracting.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Course of performance: single occasion

q: Under a requirements contract with historical orders of about 100,000 units, the buyer orders 110,000 units. The extra units are not for its own use; it plans to resell them because the market price has risen above the contract price. Which statement is correct?
o: The order may be proportionate but in bad faith.
The order is fine, because requirements contracts allow resale.
The order is unreasonably disproportionate to past orders.
The order is fine, because 110,000 is not unreasonably disproportionate.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-2's example of proportionate but bad-faith requirements: the buyer's real purpose is to resell at a higher market price.
The quantity is measured by the buyer's requirements, not by what it can profitably resell.
A 10% increase is unlikely to be disproportionate.
Proportion is only one limit; good faith is the other.
A is correct.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Proportionate but bad faith

q: A contract requires delivery by the 5th and also says: "No waiver of any term is effective unless in writing, and accepting late performance is not a waiver." The buyer accepts several late deliveries without objection. Can the seller argue the buyer waived the delivery date?
o: Courts split on whether the anti-waiver clause can itself be waived.
No, because anti-waiver clauses are enforced exactly as written.
Yes, because anti-waiver clauses are void under the UCC.
Yes, because accepting several late deliveries is a modification.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Problem 3-5(D). Some courts enforce the anti-waiver clause, while others hold the clause itself can be waived by conduct. Estoppel remains possible but weak.
Courts split.
Courts split.
Nothing suggests an agreement to modify, and conduct alone raises waiver, not modification.
A is correct.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Anti-waiver clause

q: Which of the following is a repudiation under § 2-610?
o: Failing to perform when performance is due.
Clearly indicating before performance is due that you won't perform.
Expressing doubt about your ability to perform while promising to try.
Making a written demand for adequate assurance after reasonable grounds arise.
Asking for more than the contract gives, without conditioning your own performance on it.
oe: That's a breach, not an anticipatory repudiation.
Correct. § 2-610.
A repudiation requires a clear indication you won't perform.
That is a right under § 2-609.
Not by itself a repudiation (§ 2-610 cmt. 2).
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Repudiation definition

q: Which of the following does NOT create an express warranty under § 2-313?
o: A sample or model that is made part of the basis of the bargain.
A statement purporting to be merely the seller's opinion or commendation of the goods.
A promise relating to the goods that becomes part of the basis of the bargain.
A description of the goods that is made part of the basis of the bargain.
An affirmation of fact relating to the goods that becomes part of the basis of the bargain.
oe: Correct. § 2-313(2): an affirmation merely of the value of the goods, or a statement of the seller's opinion or commendation, does not create a warranty.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Ways to create an express warranty

q: A contract says "C.I.F. Port of Baltimore." Which statement is correct?
o: Risk passes when the goods arrive at the Port of Baltimore.
It is a shipment contract, and the buyer pays against documents.
The buyer may inspect the goods in Baltimore before paying.
It is a destination contract, since the seller pays freight and insurance.
None of the above.
oe: Risk passes on shipment.
Correct. § 2-320. C.I.F. (cost, insurance, and freight) is a shipment contract: the seller ships, insures, and tenders documents, and the buyer pays against documents without inspecting first.
Under C.I.F. the buyer pays against documents.
Paying freight and insurance doesn't make it a destination contract.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — C.I.F.

q: Rowlf sells pianos to Doc's Music Hall, payment due in 60 days, and assigns the right to payment to Fraggle Bank. The bank notifies Doc. Doc then discovers the pianos are defective. Which statement is correct?
o: Doc must pay both Rowlf and the bank in full.
Doc may keep paying Rowlf until the dispute is resolved.
Doc may refuse to pay anyone until Rowlf consents to the defense.
Doc loses its defenses, because the bank took the assignment in good faith.
Doc must pay the bank but keeps its defenses against it.
oe: Doc pays once, to the assignee.
Once notified, the obligor must pay the assignee.
Doc's defenses don't depend on Rowlf's consent.
The obligor keeps its defenses against the assignee.
Correct. The assignee steps into the assignor's shoes; the obligor keeps its defenses.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Notice to obligor

q: Ace emails its buyer: "The first installment of valves will be a week late, and we expect you to cover the extra freight expenses. We'll catch up by the second installment." Is the demand for extra expenses a repudiation?
o: No, because Ace is a merchant entitled to recover costs.
No, unless Ace makes its own performance depend on the buyer's payment.
Yes, because the delay notice repudiates the whole contract.
No, because repudiation must be in a signed writing.
Yes, because Ace demanded more than the contract gives.
oe: Merchant status doesn't matter.
Correct. Problem 6-5. (The statement that installment one will be late is a definite repudiation of that installment.)
Canceling the whole requires substantial impairment of the whole contract.
Repudiation can be by words or conduct.
Demanding more is not by itself a repudiation (§ 2-610 cmt. 2).
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Demanding more

q: A seller has an output contract to sell all of its factory's production of glass jars. Which reason for shutting down the factory is LEAST likely to be in good faith?
o: A fire that destroys the factory and its equipment.
A government order closing the factory for safety reasons.
A genuine lack of orders for the seller's products.
A desire to cut its losses after the market price has risen.
None of the above.
oe: A genuine casualty is not bad faith.
That is not the seller's bad faith.
A shutdown for lack of orders can be in good faith (cmt. 2).
Correct. Comment 2: a shutdown merely to curtail losses is not good faith.
D is correct.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Shutdown

q: Gonzo's rooftop solar panels generate more electricity than his house uses, and he sells the excess to the local utility through a meter. Is the electricity a "good"?
o: Yes, because electricity is a movable thing once generated.
Yes, because Gonzo is a merchant in electricity.
No, because the utility, not Gonzo, severs the electricity.
No, because electricity is a service rather than a thing.
Maybe; courts split on metered electricity.
oe: The answer isn't that clear; courts split.
Merchant status doesn't decide whether something is a good.
Severance matters for minerals and things attached to realty (§ 2-107), not electricity.
Some courts treat metered electricity as a good; the answer is unsettled.
Correct. Problem 1-1 lists excess solar electricity as "maybe": courts split on whether metered electricity is a good or a service.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Excess solar electricity

q: Big Bird and Snuffy sign an email exchange that says: "Big Bird will sell Snuffy 300 bales of hay." The email says nothing about price or delivery. Is the record sufficient under § 2-201(1)?
o: Yes, because it is signed and states a quantity.
Yes, but both parties must be merchants.
No, because an exchange of emails can't be a signed record.
No, because it omits the price of the hay.
No, because it omits the delivery date and place.
oe: Correct. Only quantity is essential. The missing price and delivery terms are filled by the gap fillers (§§ 2-305, 2-308, 2-309).
§ 2-201(1) applies to everyone; the merchant rule is the § 2-201(2) confirmation exception.
A record includes email, and a typed name can be a signature.
Price can be missing or wrong. The record is not insufficient because it omits a term.
Delivery terms are not essential to the record.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Only quantity is essential

q: Seller contracts to sell Buyer 1,000 widgets at $10 each, delivery June 1. Seller fails to deliver. On June 1 the market price is $14. Buyer doesn't cover. What are Buyer's basic damages under § 2-713?
o: $10,000, the contract price, plus incidental damages.
Nothing, because Buyer chose not to cover.
$14,000, the market value of the widgets.
$4,000, plus incidental and consequential damages.
None of the above.
oe: That is the contract price.
Cover is optional.
That is the market value.
Correct. § 2-713: market price minus contract price, (14 − 10) × 1,000, plus incidental and consequential damages, less expenses saved.
D is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Market damages

q: Count leaves his watch with a jeweler for repair. The jeweler, who sells used watches, sells Count's watch to Zoe, who buys it in good faith in the ordinary course of business. Who has the better right to the watch?
o: Zoe, because Count entrusted the watch to a merchant in watches.
Count, because Zoe didn't get a written bill of sale from the jeweler.
Count, because he only left the watch for repair.
Count, because the jeweler had no title to pass.
Zoe, provided she paid more than the watch's market value.
oe: Correct. § 2-403(2)–(3): entrusting goods to a merchant who deals in goods of that kind gives it power to transfer all the entruster's rights to a buyer in ordinary course. The outline's example is jewelry left for repair and sold by the jeweler.
No writing is needed. The entrustment rule protects a buyer in ordinary course.
The purpose of the entrustment doesn't matter.
Entrustment gives the merchant the power to transfer the entruster's rights.
There is no such requirement.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Entrustment

q: A signed writing is a final expression of the parties' agreement on the terms it contains, but not a complete and exclusive statement. The buyer offers evidence of a prior oral agreement adding a consistent term. Is it admissible?
o: No, because the writing is a final expression of the terms.
No, because prior oral agreements are barred by a final writing.
Yes, but the writing must be ambiguous on the point.
Yes, because consistent terms may supplement a partial writing.
None of the above.
oe: Final writings can be supplemented.
Only contradictory ones are barred for a partial integration.
Ambiguity is not required for consistent additional terms.
Correct. § 2-202(b).
D is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Partial integration

q: In NIPSCO v. Carbon County Coal, an electric utility with a long-term fixed-price coal contract wanted out when it could buy power much more cheaply. What result?
o: The utility was excused because its costs became unprofitable.
The coal company had to lower its price to market.
The utility was excused by frustration of its purpose.
The utility was excused because regulators wouldn't let it pass costs through.
The utility was not excused; it bore the risk of a market drop.
oe: A fixed-price contract assigns the risk of market decreases to the buyer.
The contract price stood.
The court refused to excuse it.
That didn't change the risk allocation.
Correct. Judge Posner: a fixed-price contract assigns the risk of market decreases to the buyer, and a buyer that misforecasts the market "has only himself to blame."
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — NIPSCO

q: Gobo receives a delivery of 50 cans of paint and promptly uses 10 cans to paint his barn before discovering that the paint is the wrong color. Has Gobo accepted the paint?
o: No, because the paint did not conform to the contract.
Yes, as to the 10 cans he used, but not the other 40.
Yes, because using it is inconsistent with the seller's ownership.
No, because he hadn't finished inspecting the paint when he used it.
None of the above.
oe: A buyer can accept nonconforming goods.
If the cans are a commercial unit, acceptance of part is acceptance of the whole unit.
Use, not inspection, is the problem.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Acts inconsistent with ownership

q: A seller bears the risk of loss, and the goods are destroyed before delivery without anyone's fault. If the goods were fungible wheat, not identified at contracting, what must the seller do?
o: Nothing, because the loss of the wheat excuses its performance.
Deliver the damaged wheat at a reduced price.
Tender other conforming wheat in place of the lost wheat.
Refund the price, since the contract is avoided.
None of the above.
oe: Fungible goods don't qualify for § 2-613.
Not required or allowed.
Correct. § 2-613 applies only to goods identified when the contract was made.
Only identified goods.
C is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Fungible vs. identified

q: Which of the following is required to bind a party to a usage of trade?
o: Regular observance in the trade, plus notice to the party.
The parties must have used the practice in prior contracts with each other.
The usage must be followed universally across the industry.
The party must have expressly agreed to the usage in writing.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 1-303(c) and (g). The usage must be regularly observed in the place or trade so as to justify an expectation it will be observed, and the party must have notice of it (or be in that trade).
That describes course of dealing.
It need only be regularly observed in the place, vocation, or trade.
No express agreement is needed.
A is correct.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Usage of trade

q: Guy Smiley Rentals rents cars to the public. Every four months it sells its oldest fleet cars to the public. Does it make the implied warranty of merchantability when it sells those cars?
o: Yes, but the buyer must also be a merchant.
No, because its business is renting cars to the public, not selling them.
Yes, because it regularly and repeatedly sells used cars.
No, because the cars are used rather than new.
None of the above.
oe: The buyer's status is irrelevant to § 2-314.
Regular, recurring sales of used cars make it a merchant in cars (Problem 3-9).
Correct. Problem 3-9.
Used goods are covered, at the quality appropriate for used goods.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Rental fleet

q: A buyer orders a dining set (a table and six matching chairs) sold and priced as one set. One chair is defective. May the buyer keep the table and five good chairs and reject the defective chair?
o: No, because the set is one commercial unit.
Yes, because the perfect tender rule lets it reject any defect.
Yes, because the buyer may accept any units and reject the rest.
No, because the buyer must reject every item or none.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-606(2). A set sold as one is a commercial unit.
The perfect tender rule speaks of commercial units.
The buyer may accept or reject commercial units, not parts of them.
The buyer could reject the whole set.
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Commercial unit

q: Under § 1-201(b)(20), "good faith" means:
o: acting as a fiduciary toward the other contracting party.
reasonable care, so that a party who acts negligently acts in bad faith.
honesty in fact, judged by the party's own subjective belief.
honesty in fact and observance of reasonable standards of fair dealing.
the duty to disclose all material facts during contract negotiations.
oe: Good faith in performance is not a fiduciary duty (Market Street).
The objective prong is fair dealing, not negligence.
That is the old subjective-only definition, which some states kept in Article 1.
Correct. Good faith has a subjective prong (honesty, motive) and an objective prong (fair dealing).
Good faith applies to performance and enforcement, not negotiation.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Good faith definition

q: Rizzo sells Pepe a used outboard motor. Rizzo says: "This motor has 200 hours on it." In fact it has 2,000 hours. Rizzo never used the words "warrant" or "guarantee," and he did not intend to make a warranty. Has Rizzo made an express warranty?
o: No, because Rizzo did not use the word "warrant" or "guarantee."
No, because Rizzo did not intend to make a warranty.
Yes, because "200 hours" is a specific affirmation of fact.
No, because a used motor is sold without warranties.
No, because Rizzo is not a merchant in outboard motors.
oe: § 2-313(2): formal words such as "warrant" or "guarantee" are not required.
No specific intention to make a warranty is required.
Correct. "200 hours" is specific and measurable, it relates to the goods, and it became part of the basis of the bargain.
Used goods can carry express warranties.
Any seller can make an express warranty. Merchant status matters for § 2-314.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — No magic words

q: Sam Eagle buys a 10-year-old pickup truck from a used-car dealer. Which statement about the implied warranty of merchantability is correct?
o: The warranty arises and requires the truck to perform like a new truck.
No merchantability warranty arises, because the truck is used.
The warranty arises only if the dealer expressly says the truck is in good condition.
The warranty arises only if Sam Eagle is also a merchant.
The warranty arises, but only to the quality appropriate for used goods of that kind.
oe: The standard is adjusted for used goods.
The warranty applies to used goods.
That would be an express warranty. Merchantability is implied.
The buyer's status is irrelevant to § 2-314; only the seller must be a merchant in goods of that kind.
Correct. A used-car dealer is a merchant in cars, and the warranty applies at the level of quality appropriate for used goods.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Used goods

q: Count von Count signs a memo stating: "I agree to buy 100 wooden abacuses from Rizzo at $10 each." Rizzo claims the parties actually agreed orally to 150 abacuses. Assuming Rizzo proves the oral deal, how many abacuses can Rizzo enforce?
o: 150, because the memo is sufficient and Rizzo has proved the actual quantity.
None, because the memo misstates the quantity agreed.
125, as a compromise between the two quantities.
100, the quantity shown in the signed memo.
None, because Rizzo himself did not sign the memo.
oe: The contract is not enforceable beyond the quantity shown in the record (§ 2-201(1)).
A misstated term doesn't make the record insufficient. It caps enforcement at the stated quantity.
There is no compromise rule.
Correct. The contract is not enforceable beyond the quantity shown in the record (§ 2-201(1)). A record isn't insufficient because it misstates a term, but enforcement stops at the stated quantity.
The record must be signed by the party against whom enforcement is sought, which is the Count.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Quantity limit

q: A buyer signs a contract to buy exactly 50,000 square feet of carpet per year for three years. In year two, its business slows, and it wants to buy only 20,000. Can it?
o: No, because the contract is for a fixed quantity.
Yes, because quantity is measured by its good-faith requirements.
Yes, if it notifies the seller within a reasonable time.
Yes, because a 60% drop is not unreasonably disproportionate.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Problem 4-1(a). Without the seller's assent, the buyer bears the risk of reduced demand under a fixed-quantity contract.
This is a fixed-quantity contract, not a requirements contract.
Notice doesn't change a fixed quantity.
The disproportion rule applies to output and requirements contracts, not fixed-quantity contracts.
A is correct.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Fixed quantity

q: Seller fails to deliver 500 chairs at $40. Buyer promptly and reasonably buys substitute chairs at $50. What may Buyer recover under § 2-712?
o: $25,000, the cost of the substitute chairs.
$5,000 (cover price minus contract price), but no incidental or consequential damages.
$20,000, the contract price for the chairs.
Nothing, because Buyer got the chairs it needed.
None of the above.
oe: Buyer recovers only the difference.
A covering buyer also recovers incidental and consequential damages (§ 2-712(2)).
Not the measure.
Buyer had to pay more.
Correct. Buyer recovers $5,000 (cover price minus contract price, (50 − 40) × 500), plus incidental and consequential damages, less expenses saved (§ 2-712(2)).
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Cover

q: Why does a merchant seller keep the risk of loss until the buyer receives the goods?
o: Because title doesn't pass until the buyer receives them.
Because it still controls the goods and is likely insured.
Because the buyer usually hasn't yet paid the price.
Because merchants can spread losses across many sales.
None of the above.
oe: Title isn't the basis.
Correct. § 2-509 cmt. 3.
Payment doesn't matter.
Not the rationale. § 2-509 cmt. 3 focuses on control and insurance.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Rationale for merchant rule

q: Count lends his watch to his friend Bert, who does not deal in watches. Bert sells it to Zoe, who pays value in good faith. Can Count recover the watch?
o: Yes, but Count must reimburse Zoe the price she paid.
No, because Zoe is a good-faith purchaser who paid value for it.
Yes, because Bert had no title to pass and isn't a watch dealer.
No, because Count voluntarily entrusted the watch to Bert's care.
None of the above.
oe: There is no such requirement.
Bert never had voidable title; he was just a borrower.
The entrustment rule applies only to merchants who deal in goods of that kind.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Entrustment to a non-merchant

q: A signed writing is a complete and exclusive statement of the terms. The buyer offers evidence of a prior oral agreement adding a consistent term. Is it admissible?
o: No, unless the buyer is a consumer who didn't read it.
No, because the writing is complete and exclusive.
Yes, because the term doesn't contradict the writing.
Yes, if the buyer proves it by clear and convincing evidence.
None of the above.
oe: The buyer's status doesn't matter.
Correct. § 2-202(b).
Not when the writing is complete and exclusive.
The PER bars it regardless.
B is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Complete integration

q: Kermit contracts to sell Fozzie 100 standard steel I-beams for $20,000. Kermit then assigns "the contract" to Beaker Manufacturing, which accepts. Beaker tenders conforming I-beams. Which statement is correct?
o: The assignment transfers only Kermit's right to payment.
Fozzie must accept and pay Beaker, but Kermit stays liable.
Fozzie must pay Kermit, because only rights, not duties, were transferred.
Fozzie may refuse Beaker's I-beams, because he contracted with Kermit.
Kermit is released from all liability once Beaker accepts.
oe: An assignment of "the contract" also delegates the duties.

Correct. § 2-210(5); Problem 6-2(c). An assignment of "the contract" assigns Kermit's rights and delegates his duties. Fozzie must accept Beaker's conforming I-beams and pay Beaker, but Kermit remains liable if Beaker fails. Fozzie may also demand adequate assurance from Beaker (§ 2-210(6)).
Both were transferred, and Fozzie pays the assignee.
Standard I-beams: Fozzie has no substantial interest in Kermit personally performing.
Delegation never relieves the delegator.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Assignment of the contract

q: Under § 1-103(a), the UCC must be liberally construed to promote all of the following purposes EXCEPT:
o: permitting the continued expansion of commercial practices through custom, usage, and agreement.
simplifying, clarifying, and modernizing the law governing commercial transactions.
making the law uniform among the various jurisdictions.
protecting consumers from unfair terms in every sale of goods.
None of the above.
oe: Purpose (2).
Purpose (1).
Purpose (3).
Correct. Consumer protection isn't one of the three § 1-103(a) purposes; specific provisions (like § 2-302 and § 2-719(3)) and other consumer laws do that work.
D is correct.
topic: 1 · The UCC & which law governs — Purposes of the UCC

q: Elmo buys a car from Grover's Autorama, a car dealership. Elmo pays in full and receives all the title documents, but leaves the car on the lot, saying he'll pick it up Monday. Over the weekend the lot floods and the car is destroyed. Who bears the loss?
o: Grover's Autorama, but only if Elmo had not yet paid.
Elmo, because he had all the documents he needed to take possession.
Grover's Autorama, because Elmo had not yet received the car.
Elmo, because he had paid the full price for the car.
None of the above.
oe: The result is the same whether or not Elmo paid.
That isn't the test for a merchant seller.
Correct. § 2-509(3). A merchant seller still controls the goods and can insure them (cmt. 3).
Payment doesn't shift the risk.
C is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Merchant seller: buyer paid

q: Elmo repudiates his contract to buy Grover's van. Two days later, before performance is due, Elmo calls to say he will perform after all. Grover hasn't canceled, hasn't changed position, and hasn't said the repudiation was final. What is the effect?
o: It is ineffective, because a repudiation can't be withdrawn.
It is ineffective, because Elmo gave no consideration.
It is effective only if Grover consents to it.
It is effective only if made in a signed writing.
The retraction is effective and reinstates the contract.
oe: It can be retracted until the next performance is due.
No consideration is needed.
Grover's consent isn't needed if none of the bars applies.
Retraction may be by any method that clearly indicates the intent to perform.
Correct. § 2-611.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Retraction

q: Gobo contracts to buy custom sewer fittings for the town of Fraggle Rock's sewer project. The town cancels the project, and the fittings have no other use. Is Gobo excused?
o: Yes, under the common-law doctrine of frustration of purpose.
Yes, under § 2-613, because the fittings' purpose was destroyed.
No, because § 2-615 excuses only sellers, not buyers.
Yes, under § 2-616, by notifying the seller in writing.
Likely not, because the fittings themselves can still be delivered.
oe: Correct. Problem 6-8(a); § 2-615 cmt. 9; R2d § 265. The project's continuation was a shared basic assumption.
§ 2-613 covers casualty to identified goods.
§ 2-615 speaks to sellers, but common-law frustration supplements the Code (§ 1-103(b)).
§ 2-616 is the buyer's response to a seller's § 2-615 notice.
That isn't the issue.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Frustration of purpose

q: Abby, a florist, signs and sends Rosita an order: "Please send 1,000 tulip bulbs at $1 each." Rosita, who is not a merchant, never signs anything. Later Abby refuses to accept the bulbs, and Rosita sues. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Rosita can satisfy § 2-201(1) because Abby signed a sufficient record.
Rosita wins automatically, because the statute of frauds is satisfied.
Rosita loses, because Rosita herself never signed a record.
Rosita loses, because the confirmation exception requires two merchants.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Abby's signed order shows a contract for sale and states a quantity.
Satisfying the statute of frauds only opens the courthouse door. Rosita still must prove the contract.
Only the party against whom enforcement is sought must sign.
Rosita doesn't need the exception. Abby's own signed record satisfies § 2-201(1).
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Signed by party to be charged

q: Rosita orders 1,000 blue bottles for her bottling business. Seller delivers 1,000 bottles, 20 of which are slightly cracked. The contract is not an installment contract. Which option is available to Rosita?
o: She may reject all, accept all, or accept some commercial units.
She must accept them all and sue for damages.
She may reject only if the defect substantially impairs the value of the shipment.
She must accept them, because the defect is only minor.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. § 2-601.
She may choose.
That is the installment contract standard (§ 2-612).
The perfect tender rule lets the buyer reject if the goods "fail in any respect."
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Perfect tender

q: Which, if any, of the following language effectively disclaims the warranty of good title?
o: "Seller disclaims any warranty of title."
"These goods are sold AS IS."
"THERE ARE NO IMPLIED WARRANTIES WITH THIS SALE."
All of the above.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Specific language works.
"As is" disclaims only implied warranties under § 2-316, and the title warranty isn't one of them.
The title warranty is disclaimed only by specific language or circumstances (§ 2-312(2)).
Only A works.
A works.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Title disclaimer

q: Buyer accepts a machine warranted to produce 100 units per hour. It produces 70. The machine as warranted would have been worth $50,000; as delivered it is worth $35,000. Buyer paid $45,000. What are Buyer's direct damages under § 2-714(2)?
o: None of the above.
oe: Buyer kept the machine.
That compares the price to the value as warranted.
That subtracts the value as accepted from the price paid, which isn't the formula.
Correct. § 2-714(2): value as warranted minus value as accepted, $50,000 − $35,000. The price paid is irrelevant to this formula.
D is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Accepted nonconforming goods

q: Which of the following statements about the § 1-304 duty of good faith is NOT correct?
o: It cannot be disclaimed by agreement.
It does not apply to negotiations before the contract is formed.
The parties may set standards for measuring good faith if they are not manifestly unreasonable.
It creates an independent cause of action that can override an express contract term.
It applies to the performance and enforcement of every contract under the UCC.
oe: Correct statement (§ 1-302(b)).
Correct statement. The duty attaches to performance and enforcement.
Correct statement (§ 1-302(b)).
Correct: this statement is NOT correct. Good faith is a lens for interpreting and performing the agreement. It is not a stand-alone claim, and it cannot contradict express terms.
Correct statement (§ 1-304).
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Good faith: limits

q: Fozzie repudiates his contract to buy 100 whoopee cushions from Kermit. Kermit promptly sells them to another buyer and tells Fozzie the deal is off. Fozzie then tries to retract. Is the retraction effective?
o: No, because a repudiation can't be withdrawn once made.
Yes, if Fozzie pays a premium for the inconvenience.
No, because Kermit canceled and materially changed position in reliance.
Yes, because performance is not yet due under the contract.
Yes, because Kermit never sued on the repudiation.
oe: It is allowed unless one of the bars applies.
The bars are absolute.
Kermit's acts cut off the right to retract.
A suit isn't required to cut off retraction.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Retraction cut off

q: A buyer's new tractor is claimed by a third party who says it was stolen. The claim turns out to be unfounded, but the buyer had to defend it. Under the majority view, has the seller breached the warranty of title?
o: Only if the seller is a merchant in tractors.
No, because the title turned out to be good after all.
Yes, because a colorable claim breaches the warranty of title.
No, because the seller did not know of the claim at the sale.
None of the above.
oe: Every seller makes the warranty of title.
Most courts hold that a colorable claim breaches even if title proves good.
Correct. § 2-312 cmt. 1. The buyer shouldn't have to litigate to protect its title.
Knowledge is not required.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Colorable claim

q: A buyer's bank is seized by regulators, and the buyer's account is frozen. Is the buyer excused from paying?
o: Yes, by frustration of purpose, since the bank failure was unforeseen.
Yes, because payment became impossible through no fault of the buyer.
Yes, under § 2-615, as an unforeseen contingency.
No, and the seller may sue for the price at once.
No; it must offer a commercially substantial equivalent.
oe: The buyer's purpose isn't frustrated; only its payment method failed.
The buyer must provide an equivalent.
§ 2-615 is a seller's excuse.
The buyer may offer a substantial equivalent.
Correct. Problem 6-8(b); § 2-614(2).
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Buyer's bank seized

q: At a garage sale, Paulette sells Ron a lamp for $20 and tells him he can pick it up on her porch that afternoon. Paulette puts the lamp on the porch and tells Ron it's there. Before Ron arrives, a storm destroys the lamp. Who bears the loss?
o: Paulette, because Ron never took possession.
Ron, because a non-merchant's risk passes on tender of delivery.
Paulette, because she had a duty to protect the lamp.
It is shared equally between Paulette and Ron.
None of the above.
oe: Receipt is the test for merchant sellers only.
Correct. § 2-509(3). Paulette completed tender by putting the lamp at Ron's disposition and telling him.
Once tender is complete, the risk is on the buyer.
There's no splitting.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Non-merchant seller: tender

q: A hardware store sells a ladder that has a hidden manufacturing defect. The store had no way to discover the defect. The ladder collapses on ordinary use. Is the store liable for breach of the implied warranty of merchantability?
o: No, because the store was not negligent in selling it.
Yes, because the seller's lack of knowledge is no defense.
Yes, provided the store knew or should have known of it.
No, because the store didn't manufacture the ladder.
None of the above.
oe: Merchantability is strict liability, not negligence-based.
Correct. Merchantability is a form of strict liability: the warranty is breached if the goods were defective at the time of sale.
Knowledge is not required.
A retailer that deals in ladders makes the warranty even if it didn't make the goods.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Strict liability

q: While selling Miss Piggy a scarf, the boutique clerk says: "This looks fabulous on you." The scarf later fades in the wash. Did the clerk's statement create an express warranty?
o: No, because express warranties must be in writing.
No, because it is mere opinion or commendation (puffing).
No, because the clerk didn't use the words "warrant" or "guarantee."
Yes, because it was made by a merchant.
Yes, because Miss Piggy relied on it.
oe: Oral statements can be express warranties.
Correct. "Looks good on you" is the casebook's example of puffing (Problem 3-6). It is general, unmeasurable, and says nothing about colorfastness.
Formal words aren't required (§ 2-313(2)). The statement fails because it is opinion, not because of its wording.
Merchant status does not turn opinion into fact.
Reliance alone doesn't make a statement of opinion a warranty.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Puffing

q: A signed writing is a final expression of the parties' agreement. The buyer offers evidence of a prior oral agreement contradicting a written term. Is it admissible?
o: No, unless the seller is a merchant who drafted the writing.
Yes, if the writing is only partially integrated.
No, because a final writing can't be contradicted by prior terms.
Yes, if the oral agreement was made the same day as the writing.
None of the above.
oe: Merchant status doesn't matter.
Contradictory prior evidence is barred even for partial integrations.
Correct. § 2-202.
Contemporaneous oral contradictions are also barred.
C is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Contradiction

q: On March 1, Kermit, a banjo dealer, signs and sends Fozzie a letter: "I will sell you 10 banjos at $200 each. This offer will remain open for six months." Fozzie pays nothing for the promise. On July 1, before Fozzie accepts, Kermit revokes. Is the revocation effective?
o: Yes, because Fozzie gave no consideration, so the offer was revocable at any time.
Yes, because firm offers must be made on the offeree's form.
No, because Kermit promised in a signed writing to keep the offer open for six months.
No, because Fozzie is a merchant too.
Yes, because the firm offer's irrevocability lasted only three months.
oe: For a merchant's signed firm offer, no consideration is needed during the first three months. Before June 1 a revocation would have been ineffective.
There is no such requirement. A form supplied by the offeree just needs the offeror's separate signature.
A firm offer cannot be irrevocable for longer than three months without consideration (§ 2-205).
Only the offeror must be a merchant, and the three-month cap applies regardless.
Correct. § 2-205: the period of irrevocability is the time stated or a reasonable time, but never more than three months. By July 1 the three months had run.
topic: 2 · Formation — Firm offer: three-month cap

q: Big Bird and Snuffy agree in writing that Big Bird will buy 100 bushels of birdseed from Snuffy, with "price to be agreed." They intend to be bound, but they never agree on a price. Which statement is correct?
o: The price is the average of what each party proposed.
Snuffy may set any price he chooses.
There is no contract, because price is an essential term.
The price is whatever Snuffy charged other customers last year.
The price is a reasonable price at the time for delivery.
oe: There is no averaging rule.
A price set by one party must be set in good faith, and this contract didn't give Snuffy that power.
An open price doesn't defeat a contract if the parties intended to contract (§ 2-305(1)).
The gap filler is a reasonable price at the time for delivery, not a past price.
Correct. § 2-305(1)(b): when the price is left to be agreed and the parties fail to agree, it is a reasonable price at the time for delivery.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Open price

q: Grover's supplier delegates its duty to deliver Grover's monthly shipments to a new, unknown supplier. Grover is worried. What may Grover do?
o: Refuse to accept conforming goods from the new supplier.
Nothing, because a delegation never affects the other party.
Cancel the contract immediately, because delegation is a repudiation.
Demand adequate assurance of performance from the new supplier.
Withhold payment for past deliveries until assured.
oe: Not without a substantial interest in the original supplier's performance.
§ 2-210(6) expressly gives Grover the right to demand assurance.
Delegation alone isn't a breach or a repudiation.
Correct. § 2-210(6): Grover may treat the delegation as reasonable grounds for insecurity and demand adequate assurance.
Past deliveries were properly made and must be paid for.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Insecurity from delegation

q: Under § 2-305(2), when a contract gives one party the power to fix the price, that party must:
o: fix the price in good faith.
obtain the other party's approval.
fix a price no higher than its price for the prior year.
fix the lowest price on the market.
fix a price within 10% of the market price.
oe: Correct. § 2-305(2). Comment 3 adds that in the normal case a posted or market price satisfies good faith.
Approval is not required.
There is no such cap; the test is good faith.
Good faith doesn't require the lowest price; Comment 3 treats a posted or market price as good faith in the normal case.
There is no percentage rule.
topic: 7 · Quantity & price — Price set by one party

q: Which of the following circumstances is most likely to exclude the warranty of title without any express disclaimer?
o: A sheriff's sale of seized goods.
A sale between two consumers at a yard sale.
A sale by a used-car dealer.
A sale at a discount price.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Circumstances that give the buyer reason to know the seller doesn't claim title, like sheriff's, executor's, or police auctions, exclude the warranty (§ 2-312(2)).
Every seller makes the title warranty.
An ordinary dealer makes the warranty.
A low price alone isn't enough.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Title disclaimer by circumstances

q: Which of the following is NOT required for a firm offer under § 2-205?
o: The offer by its terms gives assurance that it will be held open.
If the assurance is on a form supplied by the offeree, the offeror separately signs it.
The offeree is a merchant.
The offeror is a merchant.
The offer is in a signed record.
oe: Required.
Required in that situation (§ 2-205).
Correct. Only the offeror must be a merchant. The offeree can be anyone.
Required. § 2-205 applies only to "an offer by a merchant."
Required.
topic: 2 · Formation — Firm offer: who must be a merchant

q: Under a lease, Tenant may buy the property at a bargain price if Landlord refuses Tenant's request to finance improvements. Tenant knows that Landlord's manager has forgotten this clause. Tenant sends a financing request without mentioning the clause, Landlord refuses, and Tenant exercises the bargain option. Under Market Street Associates v. Frey, what is the most likely result?
o: Tenant wins, because Landlord is charged with knowing its own contract.
Tenant wins, because good faith never applies once a contract is signed.
Tenant wins, because good faith governs only the negotiation of a contract.
Tenant loses, because good faith requires Tenant to act as Landlord's fiduciary.
None of the above.
oe: Market Street rejected that view where the other side deliberately exploits a known oversight.
The duty of good faith applies to performance.
Backwards. Good faith governs performance and enforcement, not negotiation (§ 1-304).
Good faith lies between a fiduciary duty and merely avoiding fraud.

Correct. Tenant loses if it deliberately took advantage of Landlord's oversight about its contract rights when it could have corrected it at no cost. That is opportunistic "sharp dealing" in performance (Market Street). The other choices either misstate when good faith applies or overstate it as a fiduciary duty.
topic: 4 · Good faith, modification, waiver & estoppel — Market Street: after contracting

q: Both parties' forms say the contract is "complete and exclusive." The buyer offers evidence of a usage of trade that supplements the terms. Is it admissible?
o: Yes, but the writing must be ambiguous on that point.
No, because usage of trade can only explain, not supplement.
No, because both forms say the writing is complete and exclusive.
Yes, because trade usage can supplement even a complete writing.
None of the above.
oe: Ambiguity is not required for UoT (cmt. 1(c)).
It can supplement.
CoD, UoT, and CoP can supplement even a complete writing.
Correct. § 2-202(a); Problem 5-12(a).
D is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Usage of trade and complete integration

q: Under § 2-314(2), merchantable goods must at least:
o: be fit for the particular purpose the buyer has in mind.
conform to any affirmations of fact on the label.
meet every safety rating at the top of their class.
be the highest-quality goods of their kind on the market.
All of the above.
oe: That is the § 2-315 warranty, not merchantability.
Correct. That is § 2-314(2)(f), alongside passing without objection, fair average quality, fitness for ordinary purposes, even kind and quality, and adequate packaging and labeling.
A car that meets all safety rules but rates low in crash tests is likely still merchantable (Problem 3-10).
Merchantability is a minimum standard.
Only B is a requirement.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Merchantability: requirements

q: Snuffy, a grain dealer, contracts to sell wheat to Big Bird and to deliver it to Big Bird's farm. Snuffy drives the wheat in his own truck, which catches fire on the way. Who bears the loss?
o: Big Bird, because the wheat was delivered to a carrier.
Big Bird, because the wheat had been identified to the contract.
Snuffy, because Big Bird never received the wheat.
Snuffy, provided he was negligent in transporting it.
None of the above.
oe: The seller's own truck isn't a carrier.
Identification doesn't pass the risk.
Correct. Problem 4-6(a). The seller's own truck is not a carrier, so a merchant seller's risk passes only on the buyer's receipt. Since wheat is fungible, Snuffy must re-tender.
Risk of loss doesn't turn on fault here.
C is correct.
topic: 9 · Risk of loss — Seller's own truck

q: Grover's supplier repudiates in a way that substantially impairs the value of the contract to Grover. What may Grover do under § 2-610?
o: Demand a higher price to cover the added risk.
Suspend performance and either wait or pursue his remedies.
Only wait until the delivery date and then sue.
Only sue immediately for anticipatory breach.
Nothing until the delivery date passes, since the supplier may still perform.
oe: Not a § 2-610 remedy.
Correct. § 2-610: suspend his own performance and either await performance for a commercially reasonable time or resort to any remedy for breach.
Grover may also resort to remedies immediately.
Grover may also wait.
Anticipatory repudiation gives immediate rights.
topic: 15 · Insecurity & repudiation — Options after repudiation

q: Kermit and Fozzie, both merchants, orally agree that Fozzie will buy 600 rubber chickens from Kermit for $3,000. The next day Kermit sends Fozzie a signed letter: "This confirms our deal: 600 rubber chickens at $5 each." Fozzie reads the letter but never responds. Three weeks later, Fozzie refuses to perform. Can Kermit enforce the contract against Fozzie?
o: No, because the confirmation was sent after the oral deal.
Yes, because Fozzie failed to object to the confirmation in time.
No, because Fozzie had 30 days to object and only three weeks passed.
Yes, because Fozzie admitted the deal by staying silent.
No, because Fozzie never signed anything himself.
oe: A confirmation is supposed to follow the oral deal.

Correct. § 2-201(2): between merchants, a confirmation sent within a reasonable time, sufficient against the sender, received by a recipient with reason to know its contents, binds the recipient unless written objection is given within 10 days.
The objection period is 10 days.
The admission exception requires an admission in court (§ 2-201(3)(b)). Silence works only through § 2-201(2).
The merchant's confirmation exception lets the sender's signed confirmation bind the recipient.
topic: 3 · Statute of frauds & unconscionability — Merchant's confirmation

q: Buyer wrongfully rejects 100 tables at $200. Seller resells them in a commercially reasonable manner for $150 each. What may Seller recover under § 2-706?
o: Nothing, because Seller resold the tables in a reasonable manner.
$20,000, the full contract price.
$15,000, the resale proceeds.
$5,000, plus incidental damages, less expenses saved.
None of the above.
oe: Seller still lost $50 per table.
That's the contract price for goods the seller resold.
That's the resale proceeds.
Correct. § 2-706: contract price minus resale price, (200 − 150) × 100, plus incidental damages, less expenses saved.
D is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Seller's resale

q: At an estate sale, Abby buys a table described on the price tag as an "antique oak table." It turns out to be a recent reproduction. Has the seller made an express warranty?
o: No, because the price tag was not signed by the seller.
Yes, because the description became part of the basis of the bargain.
No, because an estate seller is not a merchant.
No, because "antique" is only a matter of opinion.
None of the above.
oe: An express warranty needs no signature.
Correct. § 2-313(1)(b). "Antique," like "Queen Anne" or "Ming," is a description (Problem 3-6).
Any seller can make an express warranty by description.
Whether a table is an antique is a verifiable fact.
B is correct.
topic: 5 · Express warranties — Description

q: Doc orders custom gears from a machine shop and furnishes detailed specifications. A third party claims the gears infringe its patent. Which statement is correct?
o: The machine shop breached the warranty against infringement.
The patent holder must sue the buyer, not the seller.
The buyer must hold the seller harmless against the claim.
No warranty arises, because the machine shop is a merchant.
None of the above.
oe: When the buyer furnishes specifications, the warranty runs the other way.
That's not the point of § 2-312(3).
Correct. § 2-312(3): a buyer who furnishes specifications to the seller must hold the seller harmless against claims arising from compliance with them.
The non-infringement warranty is made by a merchant regularly dealing in goods of the kind.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Gap fillers & implied warranties — Non-infringement

q: Under a contract for 12 monthly deliveries of cheese, one installment arrives with a minor labeling defect that the seller can easily fix. May the buyer reject that installment?
o: Yes, because the label doesn't perfectly match the contract.
No, because a buyer can't reject a single installment.
Yes, because the buyer may reject any installment that fails in any respect.
Yes, and the buyer may also cancel the whole contract.
No, because the defect doesn't substantially impair it and can be cured.
oe: Installment contracts follow § 2-612.
They may if the substantial-impairment test is met.
That is the perfect tender rule (§ 2-601), which § 2-612 displaces for installment contracts.
Cancelling the whole requires substantial impairment of the whole contract.
Correct. § 2-612(2): in an installment contract, the buyer may reject an installment only if the nonconformity substantially impairs its value and cannot be cured.
topic: 8 · Delivery, inspection & payment — Installment contract

q: A contract has a force majeure clause excusing performance for "any labor strike." The seller's workers strike. What governs?
o: The force majeure clause, because the parties' agreement controls.
The common law of impossibility, which the clause can't displace.
§ 2-615 alone, because it sets the Code's excuse standard.
Whichever rule the buyer chooses to invoke.
Nothing; a strike is foreseeable, so it never excuses.
oe: Correct.
The contract controls.
The excuse rules yield to the parties' agreement.
The clause governs.
The clause can make them excuse.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Force majeure

q: A contract bars all assignments. Seller fully performs by delivering the goods, and Buyer fails to pay. Can Seller assign its right to payment?
o: No, because the contract bars all assignments of any kind.
Only after Seller first sues Buyer for the price.
Only with Buyer's written consent to the assignment.
Yes, because the right arises from Seller's full performance.
None of the above.
oe: The bar doesn't reach a right arising from full performance.
There is no such requirement.
No consent is needed.
Correct. § 2-210(2): a right arising from the assignor's full performance can be assigned despite an agreement otherwise. (§ 9-406(d) reaches the same result for a right to payment.)
D is correct.
topic: 13 · Assignment & delegation — Right from full performance

q: After signing a complete and exclusive written contract, the parties orally agree to change the delivery date. Does the parol evidence rule bar evidence of this agreement?
o: Yes, unless the later change is put in writing.
Yes, because the writing is complete and exclusive.
No, because the rule doesn't reach later agreements.
No, provided the buyer is a consumer who relied on it.
None of the above.
oe: The PER doesn't apply; a NOM clause or the SOF might.
The PER covers only prior and contemporaneous agreements.
Correct. The PER covers only prior and contemporaneous agreements. A later agreement is a modification, governed by § 2-209.
Status doesn't matter.
C is correct.
topic: 12 · Parol evidence rule — Later agreements

q: A piano dealer with unlimited supply contracts to sell a piano for $5,000. The buyer repudiates, and the dealer sells the same piano to another customer for $5,000. Under § 2-708(2), what can the dealer recover?
o: The full $5,000 price, since the buyer repudiated.
Its lost profit on the first sale, as a lost-volume seller.
The market price minus the contract price.
Nothing, because it resold the piano at the same price.
None of the above.
oe: The dealer still has the piano or its proceeds.
That's zero and inadequate here.
A lost-volume seller would have made both sales.
B is correct.
topic: 11 · Remedies & remedy limitations — Lost volume

q: To disclaim the implied warranty of merchantability under § 2-316(2), a seller must:
o: obtain the buyer's separate signature on the disclaimer.
mention merchantability and, if written, make it conspicuous.
use both the words "fitness" and "merchantability."
use the words "as is" and also mention fitness.
put the disclaimer in a signed writing.
oe: A separate signature is required for a NOM clause on a merchant's form (§ 2-209(2)), not for a disclaimer.
Fitness is a separate warranty.
"As is" is a separate route under § 2-316(3)(a), and mentioning fitness isn't required to disclaim merchantability.
An oral disclaimer can work.
topic: 10 · Variation by agreement & warranty disclaimers — Merchantability disclaimer

q: What is the difference between excuse and risk of loss?
o: Excuse decides who pays damages; risk of loss, who absorbs the goods' value.
Risk of loss applies only to services, excuse only to goods.
Risk of loss decides who pays damages; excuse, who absorbs the goods' value.
Nothing; they are two names for one doctrine.
Excuse applies only to buyers, risk of loss to sellers.
oe: Correct.
Risk of loss is about goods.
Reversed.
Different questions.
Excuse applies to sellers too.
topic: 16 · Excuse from performance — Excuse vs. risk of loss

q: Snuffy signs a contract to buy a skid loader from Big Bird's Equipment. The contract says nothing about delivery. Big Bird tells Snuffy the loader is ready at its lot. Snuffy refuses to pick it up, insisting Big Bird deliver it. Who is in breach?
o: Big Bird, because by default a seller must deliver the goods to the buyer's farm.
Neither, because the contract fails for indefiniteness.
Big Bird, because delivery terms must be in writing.
Snuffy, because the default place of delivery is the seller's place.
None of the above.
oe: The gap filler says otherwise.
Open terms don't defeat a contract (§ 2-204(3)).
There's no such rule.
Correct. § 2-308; Problem 3-8(A).

q: A seller tells the buyer, "Your goods are ready for pickup." Before the buyer arrives, a fire destroys them. What decides who bears the loss?

Whether title has passed.
Whether the buyer has paid.
Whether the seller is a merchant.
None of the above.
oe: Insurance is a rationale for the rule, not the test.
Risk is not tied to title.
Payment doesn't affect risk under § 2-509(3).
Correct. Problem 4-6(b): a merchant seller bears the loss because the buyer hasn't received the goods; a non-merchant seller doesn't, because tender is complete.

q: An oil company sets the price its franchise dealers must pay for gasoline. The price is within the range competitors charge, but the dealers prove the company set it in order to drive them out of business. How do courts divide on whether the price was set in good faith under § 2-305(2)?
o: All courts hold a price within the competitive range is in good faith.
Courts agree that § 2-305(2) doesn't apply to franchise agreements at all.
All courts hold that an improper motive always establishes bad faith in pricing.
Courts split; Mathis looked at motive, but most courts look only at the price.
None of the above.
oe: Mathis v. Exxon held otherwise.
Mathis applied it.
Shell v. HRN and Autry v. BP reject that view.

Correct. Mathis v. Exxon held that an intent to drive dealers out takes the case outside Comment 3's safe harbor, but the majority (Shell v. HRN; Autry v. BP) holds a commercially reasonable, non-discriminatory price is in good faith regardless of motive.

q: Miss Piggy, who owns a boutique, tells Gonzo in person: "I'll hold this gown for you at $900 until Friday." On Wednesday she sells it to someone else. Gonzo shows up Thursday ready to buy. Was Miss Piggy's offer irrevocable until Friday?
o: Yes, because she is a merchant.
No, because only a signed record makes a firm offer.
No, because Gonzo is not a merchant.
No, because a firm offer must last at least three months.
Yes, because she stated a specific time.
oe: Merchant status alone is not enough. § 2-205 requires a signed record.
Correct. An oral assurance is not a firm offer under § 2-205. Without consideration (an option contract), it was revocable.
The offeree need not be a merchant.
Three months is the maximum, not a minimum.
Stating a time is part of the test, but the assurance must be in a signed record.

Kermit sends Snuffy a signed letter confirming the deal and its quantity. Snuffy reads it and never objects. Does § 2-201(2) make the contract enforceable against Snuffy?
o: Yes, because Snuffy failed to object within 10 days.
Yes, because the sender is a merchant.
No, because Snuffy objected too late.
No, because confirmations must be signed by both parties.
None of the above.
oe: The 10-day rule binds only a merchant recipient.
Both parties must be merchants.
Snuffy never objected, and he didn't need to. The 10-day objection rule binds only a merchant recipient.
The confirmation need only be sufficient against the sender.
Correct. § 2-201(2) applies only to a contract "between merchants." Snuffy is not a merchant, so his silence doesn't bind him, and Kermit needs a record signed by Snuffy or another exception.

Sue Buyer for wrongful rejection of the goods.
Seasonably notify Buyer and cure by June 30.
Demand payment for the goods less a price allowance.
Nothing, because Buyer's rejection ends the contract.
oe: Buyer rightfully rejected and owes nothing for the nonconforming goods.
The rejection was rightful.
Correct. § 2-508(1): the seller may seasonably notify the buyer of its intent to cure and make a conforming delivery within the contract time.
Buyer rightfully rejected and owes nothing for those goods.
Seller may cure within the contract time.

No, because he can't identify the specific defect that caused the failure.

No, because the mower worked properly when he bought it.

None of the above.

That is bad faith in performance.
The remand court found exactly this to be bad faith.

There is no warranty unless Mokey relied on Gobo's expertise.

A sample creates an express warranty.

o: Yes, because contract rights are freely assignable.

Even without a prohibition, § 2-210(2) blocks assignments that materially change the other party's duty.
